arXiv:2412.01489v2 [math.PR] 22 Jun 2026

One- and two-particle spectral gap identities for the symmetric inclusion process and related models

Seonwoo Kim Address: Department of Mathematics, Yonsei University, Seoul, Republic of Korea Email address: seonwookim@yonsei.ac.kr and Federico Sau Address: Dipartimento di Matematica “F. Enriques”, Università degli Studi di Milano, Milano, Italy Email address: federico.sau@unimi.it
Abstract.

The symmetric inclusion process (SIP) models particles diffusing on a graph with mutual attraction. We recently showed [KS24] that, in the log-concave regime (where diffusivity dominates interaction), the spectral gap of the conservative SIP matches that of a single particle. In this paper, our main result demonstrates that this identity generally fails outside this regime, but always holds for the non-conservative SIP, regardless of the interaction strength. When this one-particle spectral gap identity breaks down, we derive sharp bounds for the gap in terms of diffusivity, and reveal a two-particle spectral gap identity in the vanishing diffusivity limit. Our approach leverages the rigid eigenstructure of SIP, refined comparisons of Dirichlet forms for arbitrary diffusivity and particle numbers, and techniques from slow–fast system analysis. These findings extend to the dual interacting diffusion known as Brownian energy process, and shed some light on the spectral gap behavior for related Dirichlet-reversible systems on general, non-mean-field, geometries.

Key words and phrases:
Spectral gap; interacting particle systems; Dirichlet distribution; symmetric inclusion process; Brownian energy process
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 60K35; secondary 60J27, 05C50.

1. Introduction

The symmetric inclusion process (SIP{\rm SIP}) is a system of interacting particles hopping on the sites x,y,z,…∈Vx,y,z,\ldots\in V of a finite graph GG. In its conservative version, each particle jumps from a site xx to another one yy at rate cx​y​(αy+ηy)c_{xy}\left(\alpha_{y}+\eta_{y}\right), where:

  • •

    cx​y=cy​x≥0c_{xy}=c_{yx}\geq 0 is a symmetric weight attached to the edge x​yxy;

  • •

    αy>0\alpha_{y}>0 is a weight attached to the arrival site yy;

  • •

    ηy∈ℕ0\eta_{y}\in\mathbb{N}_{0} denotes the number of particles sitting on yy.

While the rate cx​y​αyc_{xy}\,\alpha_{y} accounts for the free motion (or diffusion) of each particle, cx​y​ηyc_{xy}\,\eta_{y} introduces an interaction among them by favoring jumps on top of already occupied sites. Moreover, this dynamics is conservative (i.e., it preserves the total number of particles), reversible with respect to a discrete Dirichlet distribution, and irreducible as soon as the underlying graph is connected. We refer to Section 2 below for the detailed definition of the process and its properties.

For now, let us just remark that SIP{\rm SIP} arises within different contexts (e.g., as a discrete model of heat conduction [GKR07], and as a multi-type Moran model from population genetics with non-mean-field interactions), and comes with closely related models from statistical physics. For instance, by setting αy=1\alpha_{y}=1 and replacing the plus sign with a minus sign in the rates, one obtains the renowned symmetric exclusion process [Spi70]. Furthermore, SIP admits a continuous-spin counterpart, referred to as the Brownian energy process [GKRV09] (see also Section 8.1 below). This continuous-spin model, roughly speaking, describes the energies of an instance of Kac’s walk [Kac56], in which velocities evolve as interacting diffusions, rather than being instantaneously updated at random “collision” times.

In all these models, a central question is that of determining precise convergence rates to equilibrium, and, in the context of reversible processes, one of the most investigated quantities for this purpose is the so-called spectral gap.

1.1. One-particle spectral gap identity

For SIP{\rm SIP} on a graph G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) endowed with site weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V},

(1.1) gapSIP​(G,α)>0{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)>0

denotes the corresponding spectral gap, i.e., the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of (the negative of) the infinitesimal generator (see Section 2 for the precise definition). In a previous work [KS24], we established the following bounds on gapSIP​(G,α){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha) in terms of gapRW​(G,α){\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha), the spectral gap of the random walk (RW{\rm RW}) on GG which jumps from xx to yy with rate cx​y​αyc_{xy}\,\alpha_{y}: for all graphs GG and site weights α\alpha,

(1.2) (1∧αmin)​gapRW​(G,α)≤gapSIP​(G,α)≤gapRW​(G,α)​.\left(1\wedge\alpha_{\rm min}\right){\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)\leq{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)\leq{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)\;\text{.}

Here and all throughout, a∧b≔min⁡{a,b}a\wedge b\coloneqq\min\{a,b\} and αmin≔minx∈V⁡αx\alpha_{\rm min}\coloneqq\min_{x\in V}\alpha_{x}.

Notably, as soon as αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1, the inequalities in (1.2) saturate to an identity:

(1.3) gapSIP​(G,α)=gapRW​(G,α)​,αmin≥1​.{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)={\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1\;\text{.}

This one-particle reduction corresponds to a SIP{\rm SIP}-version of the celebrated Aldous’ spectral gap conjecture, originally formulated for interchange and symmetric exclusion processes in the early 90s, and settled two decades later in [CLR10]. In fact, the identity in (1.3) is extremely powerful, as it reduces, for every underlying graph GG, the spectral gap of SIP{\rm SIP} — an arbitrarily large system, as it may consist of arbitrarily many particles — to that of RW{\rm RW}, a much simpler Markov chain with finite state space VV, for which several techniques to bound the spectral gap in terms of simple features of the underlying graph GG are known (see, e.g., [SC97, MT06, LP17, Her23]). For completeness, let us emphasize that an identity like (1.3), while trivial for a system of independent particles, is not at all expected to hold for truly interacting systems. Indeed, apart from the processes treated in [CLR10], only a handful of other models were discovered to satisfy, on any geometry, a spectral gap identity involving the corresponding random walk. These models are:

  • •

    the symmetric exclusion process in contact with reservoirs in [Sal23, Sal24];

  • •

    the Binomial splitting process in [QS23, BC24].

The identity in (1.3) adds SIP{\rm SIP} to the short list above, provided that αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1 (we shall also refer to this condition as “log-concave regime”, see Remark 2.1 below).

One of our main results (Theorem 2.4) states that, without this condition on αmin\alpha_{\rm min}, this identity, in general, fails: for some graphs GG and site weights α\alpha,

(1.4) gapSIP​(G,α)<gapRW​(G,α)​.{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)<{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)\;\text{.}

In other words, the factor 1∧αmin1\wedge\alpha_{\rm min} in (1.2) cannot be generally neglected when

(1.5) αmin∈(0,1)​.\alpha_{\rm min}\in(0,1)\;\text{.}

This naturally leads us to further investigate this regime, with the twofold goal of:

  1. (1)

    deriving an alternative lower bound for gapSIP​(G,α){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha), better capturing its dependence on αmin\alpha_{\rm min};

  2. (2)

    obtaining a two-particle reduction of gapSIP​(G,α){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha), in the asymptotic regime of vanishing diffusivity α→0\alpha\to 0.

We discuss these two steps in Sections 1.2 and 1.3, respectively.

1.2. Sharp dependence on αmin\alpha_{\rm min}

In order to isolate the role of αmin\alpha_{\rm min}, let us introduce new site weights α^=ααmin\hat{\alpha}=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha_{\rm min}}. With this notation, a simple scaling argument implies

(1.6) gapRW​(G,α)=αmin​gapRW​(G,α^)​.{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)=\alpha_{\rm min}\,{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\hat{\alpha})\;\text{.}

Due to the particle interaction, the same argument does not directly apply to SIP⁡(G,α){\rm SIP}(G,\alpha). Instead, if combined with the inequalities in (1.2), the above identity yields

(1.7) αmin2​gapRW​(G,α^)≤gapSIP​(G,α)≤αmin​gapRW​(G,α^)​,αmin∈(0,1)​.\alpha_{\rm min}^{2}\,{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\hat{\alpha})\leq{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)\leq\alpha_{\rm min}\,{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\hat{\alpha})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\alpha_{\rm min}\in(0,1)\;\text{.}

Hence, if we encode the dependence on (G,α^)(G,\hat{\alpha}) through gapRW​(G,α^){\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\hat{\alpha}), the lower bound in (1.7) above would predict gapSIP​(G,α){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha) to depend on the square of αmin\alpha_{\rm min}.

Our second main result (Theorem 2.2) proves this guess to be wrong, showing that, in general, gapSIP​(G,α){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha) depends linearly, rather than quadratically as in (1.7), on αmin∈(0,1)\alpha_{\rm min}\in(0,1): for all graphs GG and site weights α\alpha,

(1.8) C​αmin≤gapSIP​(G,α)​,αmin∈(0,1)​,C\,\alpha_{\rm min}\leq{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\alpha_{\rm min}\in(0,1)\;\text{,}\;\;

where C>0C>0 is a constant depending only on GG and α^=ααmin\hat{\alpha}=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha_{\rm min}}. Indeed, in Theorem 2.2, since αmin≤1\alpha_{\rm min}\leq 1 and α^ratio=αratio\hat{\alpha}_{\rm ratio}=\alpha_{\rm ratio}, we have

(1.9) αmin​{154​α^ratio(6​e)1/α^ratio​cmin|V|2​diam​(G)}≤gapSIP​(G,α)​,\alpha_{\rm min}\left\{\frac{1}{54}\,\frac{\hat{\alpha}_{\rm ratio}}{(6e)^{1/\hat{\alpha}_{\rm ratio}}}\,\frac{c_{\rm min}}{|V|^{2}\,{\rm diam}(G)}\right\}\leq{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)\;\text{,}\;\;

where the constant inside the bracket in the left-hand side depends only on the graph structure and the constant α^\hat{\alpha}. Because of the second inequality in (1.7), the order-one dependence on αmin\alpha_{\rm min} for gapSIP​(G,α){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha) in (1.8) is sharp. As we will see, this sharpened result crucially requires to express the dependence on GG not through gapRW​(G,α^){\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\hat{\alpha}), but other features of the underlying geometry.

1.3. Two-particle spectral gap identity

All considerations made so far leave the following question unanswered: given that the spectral gap of SIP{\rm SIP} does not always coincide with that of a single particle (namely, RW{\rm RW}), does it instead coincide with the spectral gap of the kk-particle SIP{\rm SIP}, for some integer k≥2k\geq 2, independent of the underlying graph GG and site weights α\alpha?

Asking the same question for SIP{\rm SIP}’s “instantaneously thermalized” variant also known as Beta-Binomial splitting process (see, e.g., [PR26] or Section 8.2) — Pietro Caputo conjectured (personal communication) this spectral gap reduction to hold true with k=2k=2. In words, the Beta-Binomial splitting dynamics consists of, first selecting an edge x​yxy with rate cx​yc_{xy} (regardless of the particle configuration), and then letting particles sitting on xx and yy redistribute themselves according to the SIP{\rm SIP}-equilibrium, restricted to that edge. Besides being clearly related to SIP{\rm SIP}, the Beta-Binomial splitting process is the particle analogue of a model which shows up in the literature under various names, e.g., the Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti model [KMP82], a random walk on the simplex [CLL20], or (the energies of) the renowned Kac’s walk [Kac56, CCL03]. Spectral gap estimates for this model are known only on two specific geometric settings: the complete graph [CCL03, Cap08], and the segment with αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1 [CLL20]. In both cases, a spectral gap identity with k=2k=2 is indeed verified.

The aforementioned conjecture translates to the context of SIP{\rm SIP} as follows: for all graphs GG and site weights α\alpha,

(1.10) gapSIP​(G,α)=gap2​(G,α)​,{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)={\rm gap}_{2}(G,\alpha)\;\text{,}\;\;

where gapk​(G,α){\rm gap}_{k}(G,\alpha), k≥1k\geq 1, stands for the spectral gap of the kk-particle SIP{\rm SIP}. Clearly, we have gap1​(G,α)=gapRW​(G,α){\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha)={\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha) and (1.10) equivalently reads as gapk​(G,α)=gap2​(G,α){\rm gap}_{k}(G,\alpha)={\rm gap}_{2}(G,\alpha), for all k≥2k\geq 2 (cf. (2.5) and (2.10)). Moreover, in view of (1.3) and gapSIP​(G,α)≤gap2​(G,α)≤gap1​(G,α){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)\leq{\rm gap}_{2}(G,\alpha)\leq{\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha) in (2.10), the two-particle spectral gap identity in (1.10) remains to be verified only off the log-concave regime, i.e., when (1.5) holds.

We provide a partial answer in the affirmative to this conjecture, by determining spectral gap asymptotics as α→0\alpha\to 0 along directional limits (i.e., for ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 and some α^∈(0,∞)V\hat{\alpha}\in(0,\infty)^{V}, α=ε​α^\alpha=\varepsilon\hat{\alpha}; see (2.11)). The precise form of the asymptotic validity of (1.10) is the content of Theorem 2.3 below. We refer to Section 2.3 for more details, but let us briefly remark that our asymptotic analysis highlights the key role that the two-particle dynamics plays for both results in Theorems 2.3 and 2.4. We believe this point of view to be fruitful also for other related interacting systems with Gamma-like reversible measures. For more details, see Section 8.2.

1.4. Non-conservative case

So far, we discussed only closed (or conservative) systems in which inclusion particles neither get created nor annihilated. Open (or non-conservative) systems allow for this possibility, usually modeled as systems in contact with reservoirs, see, e.g., [Spo83, DEHP93, CGGR13]. For SIP{\rm SIP}, the standard choice consists of creating a particle in xx with rate ωx​θx​(αx+ηx)\omega_{x}\,\theta_{x}\left(\alpha_{x}+\eta_{x}\right), and annihilating each particle therein (if any) with rate ωx​(1+θx)\omega_{x}\left(1+\theta_{x}\right), where ωx\omega_{x} and θx\theta_{x} form a set of non-negative site parameters added to the model. For precise definitions, see Section 6.

In essence, the open SIP{\rm SIP} presents two main features: first, due to the lack of particle conservation, the configuration space now consists of a unique, countably infinite, irreducible component; second, the unique ergodic measure is reversible if the θ\theta-parameters do not depend on xx, and non-reversible if they do depend. This drastic change from reversibility to non-reversibility goes together with the emergence of a number of remarkable phenomena (e.g., currents, long-range correlations), which distinguish equilibrium from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, see, e.g., [Spo91, DMP91, KL99, Sch01].

Nevertheless, as already observed in the physics literature around thirty years ago for a large class of exactly solvable models [ADHR94] (see also [FGK20]), the “spectrum” does not depend on the θ\theta-parameters, and, thus, is the same for both equilibrium and non-equilibrium systems. The quotation marks above are required when dealing with infinite configuration spaces and corresponding generators, because the full spectrum, a priori, may include also non-eigenvalues and may depend on the underlying functional space on which the matrix/operators act. That said, this θ\theta-independence of the spectrum becomes rigorous for systems having a finite configuration space as, for instance, the symmetric exclusion process in contact with reservoirs (see Remark 6.6 below for more details).

In this article, we establish the following results for the non-conservative SIP{\rm SIP}, for any underlying graph GG and site weights α\alpha, ω\omega, and θ\theta:

  1. (1)

    Eigenfunctions of the purely absorbing system (corresponding to θ≡0\theta\equiv 0) “lift” to (generalized) eigenfunctions of SIP{\rm SIP} (with general θ\theta) associated to the same eigenvalues.

  2. (2)

    Remarkably, the spectral gap of the particle system with θ≡0\theta\equiv 0 coincides with

    (1.11) gapRW​(G,α,ω)>0​,{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha,\omega)>0\;\text{,}\;\;

    the spectral gap of the one-particle system, namely, of the random walk evolving on GG, and killed with rate ωx\omega_{x} when sitting on x∈Vx\in V (Theorem 6.1).

  3. (3)

    In the reversible case (i.e., when θ≡const.\theta\equiv{\rm const.}), the eigenfunctions obtained in 1 provide an orthonormal basis in a natural L2L^{2}-space.

Let us emphasize that step 1 holds for general θ\theta (i.e., in both reversible and non-reversible settings), while step 2 is a statement concerning the case θ≡0\theta\equiv 0 only; establishing the claim in 3 is where we need to restrict to the reversible SIP{\rm SIP}.

Putting these steps together, our main result in this non-conservative setting (Corollary 6.4) may be summarized as follows: for all graphs GG and site weights α\alpha and ω\omega,

(1.12) gapSIP​(G,α,ω,ϱ)=gapRW​(G,α,ω)​,whenever​θ≡ϱ>0​,{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\varrho)={\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha,\omega)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\text{whenever}\ \theta\equiv\varrho>0\;\text{,}\;\;

where gapSIP​(G,α,ω,ϱ){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\varrho) denotes the first gap in the spectrum of the reversible SIP{\rm SIP} with θ≡ϱ>0\theta\equiv\varrho>0, compatibly with the functional setting of step 3.

When comparing the conservative and non-conservative settings, we remark a different behavior of SIP{\rm SIP}’s spectral gap: while a system of two particles sharply captures the spectral gap of the many-particle closed SIP{\rm SIP}, the spectral gap of the open SIP{\rm SIP} is always governed (at least when θ≡const.\theta\equiv{\rm const.}) by one random walk with killing — with no constraint on the value of αmin>0\alpha_{\rm min}>0. We believe this dichotomy to hold true not just for SIP{\rm SIP}, but also for a larger class of interacting systems in statistical mechanics having Dirichlet-like steady states (see Section 8.2 for further details).

1.5. Organization of the paper

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Sections 2–5 concern the closed SIP{\rm SIP}. More specifically, Section 2 contains the model definition, the main results (Theorems 2.2–2.4), and an outline of their proofs. In Sections 3–4, we present the proof of Theorem 2.2; in Section 5, we prove the remaining two theorems from Section 2. Sections 6–7 focus on SIP{\rm SIP} in contact with reservoirs, the first one of these sections detailing the model and main results, the second one presenting the proofs of the main results therein. Finally, in Section 8, we briefly discuss some extensions of our results to discrete and continuous-spin models related to SIP{\rm SIP}. In particular, in view of the isospectrality showed in [KS24] between SIP{\rm SIP} and Brownian energy process, we derive spectral gap estimates for the latter. We conclude the paper with two appendices, in which we provide the full proofs of two technical ingredients employed in Section 5. For the reader’s convenience, we add, at the end of the paper, a notation guide collecting the main recurrent symbols.

2. Conservative SIP. Setting and main results

Unless stated otherwise, all throughout the article, our underlying geometry consists of a weighted finite graph G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}), with symmetric conductances cx​y=cy​x≥0c_{xy}=c_{yx}\geq 0 (conventionally, cx​x=0c_{xx}=0). We always assume the undirected graph GG to be connected, i.e., for all x,y∈Vx,y\in V, there exists a sequence x0=x,x1,…,xℓ−1,xℓ=yx_{0}=x,x_{1},\ldots,x_{\ell-1},x_{\ell}=y in VV such that ∏j=1ℓcxj−1​xj>0\prod_{j=1}^{\ell}c_{x_{j-1}x_{j}}>0. The length ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N} of the shortest sequence connecting two distinct sites x,y∈Vx,y\in V corresponds to their graph distance, distG​(x,y){\rm dist}_{G}(x,y). As usual, we define the diameter, diam⁡(G)∈{1,…,|V|}{\rm diam}(G)\in\{1,\ldots,|V|\}, as the largest of all pairwise distances.

2.1. Model

For a graph G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}), positive site weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha) denotes the Markov chain evolving on the configuration space

(2.1) Ξk≔{η∈ℕ0V:|η|=k}​,with​|η|≔∑x∈Vηx​,\Xi_{k}\coloneqq\left\{\eta\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{V}:|\eta|=k\right\}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\text{with}\ |\eta|\coloneqq\sum_{x\in V}\eta_{x}\;\text{,}\;\;

with infinitesimal generator given, for all f∈ℝΞkf\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}, as

(2.2) LG,α,k​f​(η)=∑x,y∈Vcx​y​ηx​(αy+ηy)​(f⁡(η−δx+δy)−f⁡(η))​,η∈Ξk​.L_{G,\alpha,k}f(\eta)=\sum_{x,y\in V}c_{xy}\,\eta_{x}\left(\alpha_{y}+\eta_{y}\right)\left(f(\eta-\delta_{x}+\delta_{y})-f(\eta)\right)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\eta\in\Xi_{k}\;\text{.}

In this formula, η−δx+δy∈Ξk\eta-\delta_{x}+\delta_{y}\in\Xi_{k} denotes the configuration obtained from η\eta by removing a particle from xx (if any) and placing it on yy. Since all particle configurations in Ξk\Xi_{k} are accessible (as the graph GG is connected and the weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V} are all positive), SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha) is irreducible. As a simple detailed balance computation shows, SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha) admits a unique reversible measure μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k}, given, for all η∈Ξk\eta\in\Xi_{k}, by

(2.3) μα,k​(η)=1Zα,k​∏x∈VΓ⁡(αx+ηx)Γ⁡(αx)​ηx!​,with​Zα,k≔Γ⁡(|α|+k)Γ⁡(|α|)​k!​.\mu_{\alpha,k}(\eta)=\frac{1}{Z_{\alpha,k}}\prod_{x\in V}\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_{x}+\eta_{x})}{\Gamma(\alpha_{x})\,\eta_{x}!}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\text{with}\ Z_{\alpha,k}\coloneqq\frac{\Gamma(|\alpha|+k)}{\Gamma(|\alpha|)\,k!}\;\text{.}

Here, Γ\Gamma denotes the usual gamma function satisfying, for all a>0a>0, Γ⁡(a+1)=a​Γ​(a)\Gamma(a+1)=a\,\Gamma(a).

Remark 2.1 (Log-concavity).

The measure μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k} in (2.3) is known as Dirichlet-Multinomial distribution of parameters k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, and is the discrete analogue of the Dirichlet distribution on the simplex Σ⊂ℝV\varSigma\subset\mathbb{R}^{V} of probability measures, see (8.1) and (8.3) below. The Dirichlet distribution is well known to be log-concave (in the sense that its probability density is of the form exp⁡(−U)\exp(-U), for some convex U:ℝV→ℝU:\mathbb{R}^{V}\to\mathbb{R}) if and only if αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1. Hence, μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k} is the discrete counterpart of a log-concave measure if and only if αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1. More directly, μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k} is a “discrete log-concave measure” also in the following sense: μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k} is the canonical measure (i.e., conditional on |η|=k|\eta|=k) of the product measure να,ϱ\nu_{\alpha,\varrho} in (6.3) below, whose Negative-Binomial marginal measures on ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0} are log-concave (i.e., να,ϱ​(ηx=ℓ)2≥να,ϱ​(ηx=ℓ−1)​να,ϱ​(ηx=ℓ+1)\nu_{\alpha,\varrho}(\eta_{x}=\ell)^{2}\geq\nu_{\alpha,\varrho}(\eta_{x}=\ell-1)\,\nu_{\alpha,\varrho}(\eta_{x}=\ell+1), for all ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 and x∈Vx\in V) if and only if αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1.

2.2. A non-asymptotic lower bound for the spectral gap

Because of irreducibility and reversibility, all |Ξk||\Xi_{k}| eigenvalues of the (negative) generator −LG,α,k-L_{G,\alpha,k} in (2.2) are real and non-negative, the smallest one being equal to zero, whereas the second one — referred to as spectral gap of SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha) and shortened as gapk​(G,α){\rm gap}_{k}(G,\alpha) — being strictly positive. Confronting with the notation from Section 1, we have

(2.4) gapRW​(G,α)=gap1​(G,α)​,{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)={\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha)\;\text{,}\;\;

For all graphs G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) and site weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, we have

To illustrate this point, take α≡ε∈(0,1)\alpha\equiv\varepsilon\in(0,1), so that αmin=ε\alpha_{\rm min}=\varepsilon and αratio=1\alpha_{\rm ratio}=1. For dd-dimensional boxes or tori of side length NN, Theorem 2.2 gives

for some C=C⁡(d,cmin)>0C=C(d,c_{\rm min})>0. This is not expected to be the correct dependence on NN. Indeed, in view of Theorem 2.3 and of the proof of Theorem 2.4, the relevant small-ε\varepsilon scale should rather be

Thus, while Theorem 2.2 is sharp in its dependence on αmin\alpha_{\rm min}, its dependence on the geometry is generally far from optimal.

Rather than optimizing these geometric constants on specific families of graphs, we keep the underlying geometry arbitrary and pass to the regime of vanishing weights α→0\alpha\to 0. In this setting, we identify the relevant asymptotic object not in terms of the spectral gap of RW⁡(G,α){\rm RW}(G,\alpha), but of the “second simplest system” on the same geometry: SIP2​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{2}(G,\alpha), namely the symmetric inclusion process with just two particles.

2.3. Spectral gap’s asymptotics

As already proved in [KS24] (see also Section 3.1 below), we have, for all graphs GG and site weights α\alpha,

The next result shows that, along directional limits α→0\alpha\to 0, i.e.,

equality is achieved in (2.10) for k≥2k\geq 2. This result is formulated along fixed positive directions; see Remark 5.15 below for the relation with general limits α→0\alpha\to 0.

For all graphs G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) and site weights α^=(α^x)x∈V\hat{\alpha}=(\hat{\alpha}_{x})_{x\in V}, we have

Let us stress that this result holds true for any graph GG, positive site weights α^\hat{\alpha}, and integer k≥2k\geq 2 (trivially, for k=2k=2). However, the case k=1k=1 is excluded for a good reason, as shown in the following result.

Theorem 2.4.

For some graphs G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) and site weights α^=(α^x)x∈V\hat{\alpha}=(\hat{\alpha}_{x})_{x\in V}, we have

This inequality provides, if combined with (2.10) and the definitions in (2.4)–(2.5), an instance of (1.4), namely, of the failure of the one-particle spectral gap identity in (1.3). The graphs GG and site weights α^\hat{\alpha} which we adopt to prove this result are far from being intricate. In fact, we take GG to be the standard dd-dimensional discrete torus, with d≥2d\geq 2 and sufficiently large size, and α^≡1\hat{\alpha}\equiv 1. These are just some of the possible examples that one could exhibit for proving (2.13). Indeed, as it will become apparent from the proof, essentially any other sparse geometry for which the random walk’s relaxation time (i.e., gapRW​(G,α)−1{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)^{-1}) is much smaller than the expected meeting time of two independent random walks initialized at equilibrium, will equally work. We refer to the subsequent section for further explanations.

2.4. Proofs outline

Recall that an inclusion particle jumps from xx to a nearest neighbor yy at rate proportional to αy+ηy\alpha_{y}+\eta_{y}. On the one hand, when non-zero, the term ηy≥1\eta_{y}\geq 1 stands for the interaction between particles on adjacent sites, which mutually attract each other, tending to stick together. On the other hand, αy>0\alpha_{y}>0 represents an independent mechanism of particle diffusion. In this sense, the regime αmin∈(0,1)\alpha_{\rm min}\in(0,1) depicts the situation in which, at least in some portions of the graph, particle stickiness dominates over diffusion.

This regime becomes particularly significant when considering the limit α→0\alpha\to 0. In this setting, SIP⁡(G,α){\rm SIP}(G,\alpha) exhibits a metastable behavior, as thoroughly studied in the last decade [GRV13, BDG17, KS21, Kim21, Kim25]. These works describe the following qualitative picture, when α=ε​α^\alpha=\varepsilon\hat{\alpha} as in (2.11). Roughly speaking, as long as particles are far from each other (i.e., at graph distance ≥2\geq 2), they perform jumps on the timescale ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}. As soon as they are at distance one, they stick together in a much shorter time, roughly of order one. These two mechanisms bring particles to meet and pile up together in large stacks (or, condensates) in a time of order ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}. Concurrently, some particles sitting on a stack would still attempt to jump to empty nearest neighboring vertices at rate ≍ε\asymp\varepsilon. While some of the attempts fail, that is, the “courageous” particle is instantaneously sucked back into a neighboring stack, some of these will succeed to attract sufficiently many particles, managing to move the whole stack. Due to the rates’ symmetry encoded in the condition cx​y=cy​xc_{xy}=c_{yx}, it is then part of the results in [GRV13, BDG17] to show that relevant jumps of entire stacks occur at times of order ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}, and that, on this timescale, stacks are effectively approximated by independent random walks on GG, each evolving at rate proportional to ε\varepsilon, and capable of coalescing (possibly in a very complicated way if three or more stacks are involved) when getting at distance one from each other. Hence, the metastable relevant part of the dynamics takes place, according to this qualitative picture, on the timescale ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}.

Although this metastable picture provides a first correct intuition that gapSIP​(G,ε​α^)≍ε{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\varepsilon\hat{\alpha})\asymp\varepsilon as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, our quantitative analysis must take into account also features not captured by usual metastability limit theorems. For instance, while metastability describes macroscopic features of the system when initialized from macroscopically relevant configurations, global functional inequalities as those determining spectral gaps require bounds which must be uniform over the initial conditions. Moreover, we seek for lower bounds for gapSIP​(G,ε​α^){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\varepsilon\hat{\alpha}) that are independent of the system size. However, a crucial ingredient in the metastability picture of SIP⁡(G,ε​α^){\rm SIP}(G,\varepsilon\hat{\alpha}) is that k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, the number of particles in the system is not too large; more precisely,

(2.14) log⁡k≪ε−1​,as​ε≪1​.\log k\ll\varepsilon^{-1}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\text{as}\ \varepsilon\ll 1\;\text{.}

This condition, always assumed in previous works (see, e.g., [GRV13, BDG17, Kim21, Kim25]) is not just technical, but strictly required for the condensation mechanism to take place: (2.14) is a sufficient and necessary condition for the steady state of the system to charge configurations consisting of a single stack of particles only.

2.4.1. Outline of the proof of Theorem 2.2

Our proof for determining the order-one dependence on ε​α^min\varepsilon\hat{\alpha}_{\rm min} of gapSIP​(G,ε​α^){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\varepsilon\hat{\alpha}) combines three main ingredients:

  • •

    the nested eigenstructure of SIP{\rm SIP} (valid for any underlying graph GG) as already exploited in [KS24];

  • •

    the full knowledge of the eigendecomposition in mean-field geometries and, more specifically, the fact that eigenvalues grow quadratically (neglecting multiplicities) with the particle total number;

  • •

    comparison inequalities of Dirichlet forms associated to the particle system on a graph GG, against that on the complete graph.

All three steps are presented and combined to yield the proof of Theorem 2.2 in Section 3, but the actual proof of the comparison inequality, longer and more technical, is presented in Section 4.

In the metastable regime (2.14), our comparisons build on the classical distinguishing paths method as applied, e.g., in the seminal work [DSC93] to the symmetric exclusion process. Most of the care in our context lies in devising paths in which the total “cost” becomes not larger than ε−1​k2\varepsilon^{-1}\,k^{2}, up to constants depending only on GG and α^\hat{\alpha}. Here, the cost of each move heavily depends on whether relocating a single particle augments, keeps constant, or lowers the total number of stacks, and whether stacks do have or not neighboring stacks. Hence, following the metastable behavior of the system offers us a guideline to construct efficient distinguishing paths, e.g., taking care of never creating more than one extra occupied site along the path. We refer to Sections 4.2 and 4.3 for the details.

When (2.14) does not hold, as already mentioned, the metastability picture breaks down, and so does this approach via distinguishing paths. In order to overcome this, we replace paths by a more sophisticated two-dimensional surface, which is obtained by collecting the trace of all relevant paths. In presence of stacks consisting of a huge number of particles, this two-dimensional surface allows us to rigorously implement the idea of moving only a smaller portion of the stack at the time according to some suitably chosen probability, and leaving the rest untouched. While this strategy of moving only some (and not all) particles of a stack produces an extra factor ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}, which we could not afford in the regime (2.14), this is now not problematic, as we can control this factor with a suitable function of the number of particles of the stack. For more details, see Section 4.4.

As we just sketched, these estimates involving Dirichlet forms yield comparison constants which unavoidably degenerate like 1/k21/k^{2} as the total number of particles k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} grows. Here is where we crucially exploit the first two ingredients of the proof, in particular, the quadratic growth of eigenvalues for the mean-field system, which removes this degeneracy.

2.4.2. Outline of the proof of Theorems 2.3 and 2.4

In order to establish the strict inequality between gapSIP​(G,ε​α^){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\varepsilon\hat{\alpha}) and gapRW​(G,ε​α^){\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\varepsilon\hat{\alpha}) as in (1.4), comparison arguments as those we just described turn out to be too loose (and, actually, too elaborated) to capture the precise pre-factors. Instead, we follow a more basic approach, namely, turning the aforementioned metastability picture into some quantitative spectral information.

More specifically, for a fixed graph GG and a fixed number of particles k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, we employ and sharpen classical limit theorems for slow–fast systems from [Kur73] (see also [GRV13] for another application in the context of SIP{\rm SIP}). These theorems rigorously describe the metastable dynamics for the slow macroscopic variables of SIP⁡(G,ε​α^){\rm SIP}(G,\varepsilon\hat{\alpha}) in the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. The limit of the slow variables after a thermalization of the fast ones identifies the low-lying spectrum. This allows us to capture the behavior of gapSIP​(G,ε​α^){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\varepsilon\hat{\alpha}), at least for ε\varepsilon small enough. These intuitive ideas are stated and proved rigorously in Section 5.1.

We are then left with identifying the spectral gap of the limiting metastable dynamics. In contrast to SIP{\rm SIP}, which is irreducible, this metastable chain may consist of both recurrent and transient states, as we detail in Section 5.2. Recurrent regions correspond to those configurations in which all particles sit together, and the resulting single stack moves like RW⁡(G,α^){\rm RW}(G,\hat{\alpha}). Transient states are those configurations in which there are stacks at graph distance at least two from each other. Hence, the spectral gap of the metastable process is just the smallest among the random walk’s gap and the eigenvalues associated to any part of the (sub-stochastic) transient dynamics.

Most of our work is devoted to analyzing the hierarchy of transient states. Indeed, even the decomposition into irreducible components and the jump rates of the transient dynamics are, in general, highly complicated and non-trivially dependent on the underlying geometry and the number of particles. Nevertheless, by exploiting a form of consistency for the metastable limiting dynamics, we are able to deduce that the lowest-lying eigenvalue of the transient dynamics is attained by the system with just two particles, as adding more particles — thus, potentially, stacks — does not cause any slowdown in the system. More in detail, in Section 5.3, we verify that one only needs to focus on the number of stacks (and not on the precise allocation of particles in each stack): for each m≥2m\geq 2, the smallest eigenvalue of all transient sub-systems with mm piles comes exactly from the sub-system with mm isolated particles. As a next step, in Section 5.4, we prove that the smallest eigenvalue of all sub-systems with m≥2m\geq 2 isolated particles is attained at m=2m=2, i.e., the sub-system with two isolated particles. Collecting these observations, we prove Theorem 2.3 in Section 5.5. Theorem 2.4 is also proved in this section: by exploiting this rigorous metastable description of eigenvalues’ asymptotics, our proof boils down to estimates of relaxation and mean meeting times of independent particles on a well studied geometry, corresponding, respectively, to (the inverse of) the spectral gap of the recurrent and transient dynamics of SIP{\rm SIP}’s metastable process.

3. Proof of Theorem 2.2

We follow the outline in Section 2.4.1.

4.4. Decomposition of gradients: empty sites & many particles

In this subsection, we assume that (4.18), (4.40) hold and that (cf. (4.41))

(4.50) αx​∑j=1m−11j>1​.\alpha_{x}\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\frac{1}{j}>1\;\text{.}

In this case, constructing a single one-dimensional path is insufficient to bound the term ∇K2​f​(σm,ℓ−mx​y,x,y){\nabla_{K}^{2}f(\sigma_{m,\ell-m}^{xy};x,y)} properly. The main reason is that in the inequality in (4.46), we are not able to bound the term eαx​∑j=1m−11je^{\alpha_{x}\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\frac{1}{j}} with a constant in this new regime (4.50). Having in mind that this term essentially comes from the mechanism that all mm particles at xx move together, we now avoid this obstacle by sending only a limited amount of particles along the path. This replacement costs us an additional αx−1\alpha_{x}^{-1} term in the upper bound, which is now manageable by the new condition αx​∑j=1m−11j>1\alpha_{x}\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\frac{1}{j}>1; we refer to (4.73) for the exact place where this point is effectively exploited.

Define a new integer m~\widetilde{m} as

(4.51) m~≔⌊m2⌋​,\widetilde{m}\coloneqq\left\lfloor\frac{m}{2}\right\rfloor\;\text{,}\;\;

where ⌊a⌋\lfloor a\rfloor is the greatest integer less than or equal to a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}. Then, we consider a two-dimensional system of paths from σm,ℓ−mx​y\sigma_{m,\ell-m}^{xy} to σm−1,ℓ−m+1x​y\sigma_{m-1,\ell-m+1}^{xy} as depicted in Figure 4.3.

In Figure 4.3, the downward vertical arrows starting from σm,ℓ−mx​y\sigma_{m,\ell-m}^{xy} in the top left corner denote the m~\widetilde{m} consecutive particle jumps from xx to x1x_{1}. Then, for i∈⟦1,m~⟧i\in\llbracket 1,\widetilde{m}\rrbracket, the ii-th bold arrow on the left, from σm−i,i,ℓ−mx​x1​y\sigma_{m-i,i,\ell-m}^{xx_{1}y} to σm−i,i,ℓ−mx​xt−1​y\sigma_{m-i,i,\ell-m}^{xx_{t-1}y}, denote the movements of ii particles from xs−1x_{s-1} to xsx_{s} consecutively for each s∈⟦2,t−1⟧s\in\llbracket 2,t-1\rrbracket, as in mechanism (F) in Section 4.3. Next, the middle horizontal arrows denote the single particle jump from xt−1x_{t-1} to yy, corresponding to mechanism (S) in Section 4.3. The bold arrows in the right part denote the movements of i−1i-1 particles from xt−1x_{t-1} back to x1x_{1} for each i∈⟦2,m~⟧i\in\llbracket 2,\widetilde{m}\rrbracket (backwards), as in mechanism (B) in Section 4.3. Finally, the upward vertical arrows below σm−1,ℓ−m+1x​y\sigma_{m-1,\ell-m+1}^{xy} in the top right corner denote the m~−1\widetilde{m}-1 consecutive particle jumps from x1x_{1} to xx. The values attached to the arrows, roughly speaking, play the role of weights (encoded as the value of the flow, see below) for each move.

As before, let Ω=Ωx,yℓ,m,σ\Omega=\Omega_{x,y}^{\ell,m,\sigma} be the collection of all edges that appear in Figure 4.3. The objective of this subsection is to prove the following lemma:

Lemma 4.6.

Assume that (4.18) holds, and suppose that ℓ∈⟦1,k⟧\ell\in\llbracket 1,k\rrbracket, m∈⟦1,ℓ⟧m\in\llbracket 1,\ell\rrbracket and σ∈Ξk−ℓV∖{x,y}\sigma\in\Xi_{k-\ell}^{V\setminus\{x,y\}} satisfy (4.40) and (4.50). Then, we have

(4.52) ∇K2f​(σm,ℓ−mx​y,x,y)≤4​t​m​(αy+ℓ−m)​ 6αmaxαmin​αratio​cmin​(∑{ζ,ζ′}∈Ω∇2f​(ζ,ζ′))​.{\nabla_{K}^{2}f(\sigma_{m,\ell-m}^{xy};x,y)}\leq\frac{{4t\,m\left(\alpha_{y}+\ell-m\right)}\,6^{\alpha_{\rm max}}}{\alpha_{\rm min}\,\alpha_{\rm ratio}\,c_{\rm min}}\left(\sum_{\{\zeta,\zeta^{\prime}\}{\in}\Omega}\nabla^{2}f(\zeta,\zeta^{\prime})\right)\;\text{.}

To derive an estimate similar to (4.43) that works also in this two-dimensional setting, we make use of some potential-theoretic arguments. We present the statements as concisely as possible and refer the readers to, e.g., [BH15, Chapter 7] or [Kim25, Appendix A] for more details about the objects used in this subsection.

Only in this subsection, we restrict the original system SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha) to the subset of the configurations that appear in Figure 4.3, which we denote by Ξ^\hat{\Xi}. Moreover, let 𝒟Ω​(g)\mathcal{D}_{\Omega}(g) denote the (normalized) Dirichlet form in Ξ^k{\hat{\Xi}_{k}} given by (cf. (4.12))

4.5. General case and proof of Theorem 3.2

Now, we handle the general case without the restrictions imposed in the previous four subsections. The idea is to send a particle from xx to yy along the sequence x=x0,x1,…,xt=yx=x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}=y by obeying the following two criteria:

  • •

    If consecutive sites are occupied by particles in σ\sigma, send a single particle along these occupied sites as explained in Section 4.2.

  • •

    If consecutive sites are empty for the configuration σ\sigma, follow the mechanism explained in Sections 4.3 or 4.4 depending on the size of the stack of particles just before these empty sites.

To state this procedure in a rigorous manner, we decompose ⟦0,t⟧{\llbracket 0,t\rrbracket} as

We further divide into three subcases according to the type — [I], [II] and [III] — of the particle jump z→wz\to w.

On the other hand, if η→η−δz+δw\eta\to\eta-\delta_{z}+\delta_{w} is of type (S), then s=s′′s=s^{\prime\prime}, and we have

    Here, both sides detect the instance right before when the single jump z→wz\to w occurs, which is clearly η\eta in the left-hand side and also the configuration in the right-hand side by the same logic as explained above. 5. Proofs of Theorems 2.3 and 2.4

In this section, we prove Theorems 2.3 and 2.4, following the outline of Section 2.4.2. The basic starting idea is to split the infinitesimal generator LG,α,kL_{G,\alpha,k} into two parts: a slow part and a fast part. In view of this decomposition, standard limit theorems for slow–fast systems ensure that, in the small-diffusivity limit, SIP\rm SIP is well approximated by the slow dynamics, after a suitable projection/thermalization according to the fast one. Understanding how and when this projection affects SIP{\rm SIP}’s spectral gap is the main non-trivial task of this section.

Recall from (2.11) that we assume α=ε​α^\alpha=\varepsilon\hat{\alpha}, where α^=(α^x)x∈V\hat{\alpha}=(\hat{\alpha}_{x})_{x\in V} are fixed site weights and ε\varepsilon tends to 00. Finally, since the graph GG is fixed all throughout the section, we often drop it from the notation, and simply write, e.g., SIPk​(α)=SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(\alpha)={\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha) and Lα,k=LG,α,kL_{\alpha,k}=L_{G,\alpha,k}.

5.1. Slow and fast dynamics

Fix k≥2k\geq 2, and consider SIPk​(ε​α^){\rm SIP}_{k}(\varepsilon\hat{\alpha}) with time sped up by a factor ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}. Recalling (2.2), the corresponding generator is then simply given by ε−1​Lα,k=ε−1​Lε​α^,k\varepsilon^{-1}L_{\alpha,k}=\varepsilon^{-1}L_{\varepsilon\hat{\alpha},k}. By separating the ε\varepsilon-dependent terms from the rest, we obtain

where, for all f∈ℝΞkf\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} and η∈Ξk\eta\in\Xi_{k},

(5.3) Bk​f​(η)\displaystyle B_{k}f(\eta) ≔∑x,y∈Vcx​y​ηx​ηy​(f⁡(η−δx+δy)−f⁡(η))​.\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{x,y\in V}c_{xy}\,\eta_{x}\eta_{y}\left(f(\eta-\delta_{x}+\delta_{y})-f(\eta)\right)\;\text{.}

Let (𝒜α^,k​(t))t≥0(\mathcal{A}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(t))_{t\geq 0} and (ℬk​(t))t≥0(\mathcal{B}_{k}(t))_{t\geq 0} denote the Markov chains in Ξk\Xi_{k} generated by Aα^,kA_{\hat{\alpha},k} and BkB_{k}, respectively. More in detail, (𝒜α^,k​(t))t≥0(\mathcal{A}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(t))_{t\geq 0} describes kk independent particles on GG, while (ℬk​(t))t≥0(\mathcal{B}_{k}(t))_{t\geq 0} is a particle system with absorbing set

and transient set Δk≔Ξk∖Ωk\Delta_{k}\coloneqq\Xi_{k}\setminus\Omega_{k}, i.e.,

5.2. Recurrent and transient states

As already proved in Proposition 5.1, 𝒢α^,k=Πk​Aα^,k|ℛ⁡(Πk):ℛ⁡(Πk)→ℛ⁡(Πk){\mathscr{G}}_{\hat{\alpha},k}=\Pi_{k}A_{\hat{\alpha},k}|_{\mathcal{R}(\Pi_{k})}:\mathcal{R}(\Pi_{k})\to\mathcal{R}(\Pi_{k}) may be interpreted as the infinitesimal generator of a Markov chain on Ωk\Omega_{k}, hereafter referred to as (ℳα^,k​(t))t≥0(\mathcal{M}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(t))_{t\geq 0}. For notational simplicity, instead of analyzing directly the operator 𝒢α^,k{\mathscr{G}}_{\hat{\alpha},k} on the |Ωk||\Omega_{k}|-dimensional subspace ℛ⁡(Πk)\mathcal{R}(\Pi_{k}) of ℝΞk\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}, we identify ℛ⁡(Πk)\mathcal{R}(\Pi_{k}) with ℝΩk\mathbb{R}^{\Omega_{k}} by restriction to Ωk\Omega_{k}, and analyze the transformed rate matrix — defined as Mα^,kM_{\hat{\alpha},k} in (5.16) or (5.37) below — on ℝΩk\mathbb{R}^{\Omega_{k}}. Let us now describe this rate matrix in detail.

Recall the chains (𝒜α^,k​(t))t≥0(\mathcal{A}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(t))_{t\geq 0} and (ℬk​(t))t≥0(\mathcal{B}_{k}(t))_{t\geq 0} introduced at the beginning of Section 5.1. Let 𝐫α^,k𝒜\mathbf{r}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\hat{\alpha},k} be the transition-rate function of the process (𝒜α^,k​(t))t≥0(\mathcal{A}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(t))_{t\geq 0}. (5.14) τξ≔inf{t≥0:ℬk​(t)=ξ}​,τΩk≔minξ∈Ωk⁡τξ​.\tau_{\xi}\coloneqq\inf\{t\geq 0:\mathcal{B}_{k}(t)=\xi\}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\tau_{\Omega_{k}}\coloneqq\min_{\xi\in\Omega_{k}}\tau_{\xi}\;\text{.}

for the corresponding square rate matrix of size |Ωk||\Omega_{k}|.

From the form of these rates, we immediately derive a classification of recurrent and transient states for this Markov chain; this will lead to a further characterization of the spectral gap wk​(α^)w_{k}(\hat{\alpha}) of 𝒢α^,k{\mathscr{G}}_{\hat{\alpha},k}. We collect this classification in Proposition 5.4 below; its direct consequence on the spectral gap is the content of the subsequent corollary. Before that, let us introduce, for every integer m≥1m\geq 1,

(5.17) Ωk,m≔{η∈Ωk:|{x∈V:ηx>0}|=m}​,\Omega_{k,m}\coloneqq\left\{\eta\in\Omega_{k}:|\{x\in V:\eta_{x}>0\}|=m\right\}\;\text{,}\;\;

that is, the set of configurations in Ωk\Omega_{k} with mm separated stacks of particles (cf. (5.4)). Clearly, Ωk,m=∅\Omega_{k,m}=\varnothing implies Ωk,m+ℓ=∅\Omega_{k,m+\ell}=\varnothing for all ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1. Further, we have Ωk,1≠∅\Omega_{k,1}\neq\varnothing, Ωk,k+1=∅\Omega_{k,k+1}=\varnothing, and, thus, Ωk=⊔m=1∞Ωk,m=Ωk,1⊔Ωk,2⊔⋯⊔Ωk,k\Omega_{k}=\sqcup_{m=1}^{\infty}\Omega_{k,m}=\Omega_{k,1}\sqcup\Omega_{k,2}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup\Omega_{k,k}.

To make the limiting dynamics more transparent, we first discuss a simple example.

Example 5.3 (Three-site path: block structure).

Let GG be the path {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\}, with conductances c12,c23>0c_{12},c_{23}>0 and c13=0c_{13}=0, and consider the limiting chain on Ωk\Omega_{k} generated by Mα^,kM_{\hat{\alpha},k}. This example illustrates the block structure described above.

For k=2k=2, the absorbing set of the fast dynamics is

The block Ω2,1\Omega_{2,1} is recurrent: it describes a single stack of two particles moving effectively as one random walk on GG. The block Ω2,2\Omega_{2,2} is transient: from δ1+δ3\delta_{1}+\delta_{3}, a slow jump of either particle to the middle site creates a configuration in Δ2\Delta_{2}, after which the fast dynamics immediately thermalizes into the recurrent block Ω2,1\Omega_{2,1}, never returning to Ω2,2\Omega_{2,2}.

For k=3k=3, one similarly has

(5.19) Ω3=Ω3,1⊔Ω3,2​,Ω3,1={3​δ1,3​δ2,3​δ3}​,Ω3,2={2​δ1+δ3,δ1+2​δ3}​,\Omega_{3}=\Omega_{3,1}\sqcup\Omega_{3,2}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\Omega_{3,1}=\{3\delta_{1},3\delta_{2},3\delta_{3}\}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\Omega_{3,2}=\{2\delta_{1}+\delta_{3},\ \delta_{1}+2\delta_{3}\}\;\text{,}\;\;

while Ω3,m=∅\Omega_{3,m}=\varnothing for all m≥3m\geq 3. Again, Ω3,1\Omega_{3,1} is recurrent, while Ω3,2\Omega_{3,2} is transient. In contrast with the case k=2k=2, however, a slow jump from a state in Ω3,2\Omega_{3,2} to Δ3\Delta_{3} need not be followed by a fast relaxation directly into Ω3,1\Omega_{3,1}: the fast dynamics may also reach the other state of Ω3,2\Omega_{3,2}. Indeed, starting, e.g., from 2​δ1+δ3∈Ω3,22\delta_{1}+\delta_{3}\in\Omega_{3,2}, a slow jump of one of the two particles sitting at site 11 to site 22 yields δ1+δ2+δ3∈Δ3\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}+\delta_{3}\in\Delta_{3}. In conclusion, for k=3k=3, the transient block is already a genuine two-state sub-Markov chain.

Remark 5.5.

The claim in Proposition 5.42 is the finite-particle analogue of the metastable picture of SIP{\rm SIP}, fully detailed in [GRV13, BDG17].

Remark 5.6.

For k≥m≥2k\geq m\geq 2, the dynamics on Ωk,m≠∅\Omega_{k,m}\neq\varnothing encoded by Mα^,kM_{\hat{\alpha},k} goes as follows. All stacks evolve as independent RW⁡(α^){\rm RW}(\hat{\alpha}) as long as their mutual distances are at least three. When two or more stacks reach mutual distance two, then there is a positive rate for them to merge. These rates — as well as the new positions of the stacks and their new compositions — depend on GG and α^\hat{\alpha}, but also non-trivially on k≥mk\geq m and, when k>mk>m, on the stacks’ composition. For more details, see Section 5.3.2 below.

The state-classification in Proposition 5.4 may be equivalently restated as follows: after a suitable conjugation with a permutation matrix, Mα^,kM_{\hat{\alpha},k} is turned into a block lower triangular matrix with Mα^,k,1,…,Mα^,k,kM_{\hat{\alpha},k,1},\ldots,M_{\hat{\alpha},k,k} as diagonal blocks, where, for all m∈⟦1,k⟧m\in\llbracket 1,k\rrbracket,

(5.24) Mα^,k,m∈ℝ|Ωk,m|×|Ωk,m|M_{\hat{\alpha},k,m}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\Omega_{k,m}|\times|\Omega_{k,m}|}

is the submatrix of Mα^,kM_{\hat{\alpha},k} obtained from the restriction on configurations in Ωk,m\Omega_{k,m} (see Figure 5.2). Since the eigenvalues of block triangular matrices are the union of those of the diagonal blocks, it suffices to focus on the spectrum of the blocks Mα^,k,mM_{\hat{\alpha},k,m}, m∈⟦1,k⟧m\in\llbracket 1,k\rrbracket. As already showed in the previous section, the eigenvalues of −Mα^,k,m-M_{\hat{\alpha},k,m}, m∈⟦1,k⟧m\in\llbracket 1,k\rrbracket, are all real and non-negative. Remark that:

  • •

    for m=1m=1, the spectrum of Mα^,k,mM_{\hat{\alpha},k,m} coincides with that of the generator of RW⁡(α^){\rm RW}(\hat{\alpha});

  • •

    for m≥2m\geq 2 and Ωk,m≠∅\Omega_{k,m}\neq\varnothing, Mα^,k,mM_{\hat{\alpha},k,m} is the rate matrix of a sub-Markovian chain killed upon exiting Ωk,m\Omega_{k,m}; thus, all its eigenvalues are strictly negative.

5.3.2. Irreducible decompositions

By an irreducible component of (ℳα^,k​(t))t≥0(\mathcal{M}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(t))_{t\geq 0} on Ωk,m\Omega_{k,m} we mean a communicating class for the restriction of the transition graph to Ωk,m\Omega_{k,m}: two configurations η,ξ∈Ωk,m\eta,\xi\in\Omega_{k,m} belong to the same component if there exist paths η=η0,η1,…,ηℓ=ξ\eta=\eta_{0},\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{\ell}=\xi and ξ=ξ0,ξ1,…,ξr=η\xi=\xi_{0},\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{r}=\eta, all contained in Ωk,m\Omega_{k,m}, such that

(5.40) 𝐫α^,kℳ​(ηh−1,ηh)>0​,𝐫α^,kℳ​(ξh−1,ξh)>0​,\mathbf{r}^{\mathcal{M}}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\eta_{h-1},\eta_{h})>0\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\mathbf{r}^{\mathcal{M}}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\xi_{h-1},\xi_{h})>0\;\text{,}\;\;

for all admissible indices. An irreducible decomposition is the partition of Ωk,m\Omega_{k,m} into such irreducible components.

The chain (ℳα^,k​(t))t≥0(\mathcal{M}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(t))_{t\geq 0} is not necessarily irreducible on Ωk,m\Omega_{k,m}. For instance, when G=𝕋2​mG=\mathbb{T}_{2m} is the one-dimensional discrete torus of size 2​m2m,

Ωm,m={δ1+δ3+…+δ2​m−1,δ0+δ2+…+δ2​m−2}≕{ηm,odd,ηm,even}{\Omega_{m,m}=\{\delta_{1}+\delta_{3}+\ldots+\delta_{2m-1},\delta_{0}+\delta_{2}+\ldots+\delta_{2m-2}\}\eqqcolon\{\eta_{m,\rm odd},\eta_{m,\rm even}\}}

consists of exactly two configurations (one with particles/stacks on the odd numbers, the other one on the even numbers), and 𝐫α^,kℳ​(ηm,odd,ηm,even)=𝐫α^,kℳ​(ηm,even,ηm,odd)=0{\bf r}_{\hat{\alpha},k}^{\mathcal{M}}(\eta_{m,\rm odd},\eta_{m,\rm even})={\bf r}_{\hat{\alpha},k}^{\mathcal{M}}(\eta_{m,\rm even},\eta_{m,\rm odd})=0. Moreover, the structure of the irreducible components of the chain (ℳα^,k​(t))t≥0(\mathcal{M}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(t))_{t\geq 0} on Ωk,m\Omega_{k,m} is always finer than the corresponding structure on Ωm,m\Omega_{m,m}, in the sense of the following proposition.

Proposition 5.12.

For all integers k≥3k\geq 3, we have

(5.63) λk,k​(α^)≥λ2,2​(α^)​,k≥2​.\lambda_{k,k}(\hat{\alpha})\geq\lambda_{2,2}(\hat{\alpha})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad k\geq 2\;\text{.}

We are ready to prove Theorems 2.3 and 2.4.

Proof of Theorem 2.3.

By Corollary 5.2 and (5.26) (we omit GG from the notation),

(5.67) limε→0gapk​(ε​α^)ε=gapRW(α^)∧minm∈⟦2,k⟧λk,m(α^),\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{{\rm gap}_{k}(\varepsilon\hat{\alpha})}{\varepsilon}={\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(\hat{\alpha})\wedge\min_{m\in\llbracket 2,k\rrbracket}\lambda_{k,m}(\hat{\alpha})\;\text{,}\;\;

Proof of Theorem 2.4.

Recall that, for all graphs GG and site weights α^\hat{\alpha}, we have gap1​(G,ε​α^)=ε​gapRW​(G,α^){{\rm gap}_{1}(G,\varepsilon\hat{\alpha})}=\varepsilon\,{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\hat{\alpha}), ε>0\varepsilon>0; moreover, by (5.67) for k=2k=2, we have

Thus, it suffices to verify the existence of GG and α^\hat{\alpha} such that

We conclude this section with a remark on the role of the directional limits in (2.11) in proving Theorem 2.3.

Theorem 2.3 is stated for directional limits α=ε​α^\alpha=\varepsilon\hat{\alpha}, with α^∈(0,∞)V\hat{\alpha}\in(0,\infty)^{V} fixed and ε→0\varepsilon\to 0; see (2.11). Let us briefly explain what would be needed in order to pass from (2.11) to a completely general limit α→0\alpha\to 0.

A natural target would be the lower bound (we omit GG from the notation)

By the sequential characterization of the liminf, it suffices to consider arbitrary sequences αn→0\alpha_{n}\to 0, as n→∞n\to\infty, in (0,∞)V(0,\infty)^{V}. By setting

(5.86) εn≔(αn)max=‖αn‖∞​,βn≔εn−1​αn​,\varepsilon_{n}\coloneqq(\alpha_{n})_{\rm max}=\|\alpha_{n}\|_{\infty}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\beta_{n}\coloneqq\varepsilon_{n}^{-1}\alpha_{n}\;\text{,}\;\;

we have εn→0\varepsilon_{n}\to 0 and, up to extracting a subsequence, βn→α^\beta_{n}\to\hat{\alpha}, for some α^∈[0,1]V\hat{\alpha}\in[0,1]^{V} with maxx∈V⁡α^x=1\max_{x\in V}\hat{\alpha}_{x}=1. Along such a subsequence, the analogue of (5.1) reads as

where Aβn,kA_{\beta_{n},k} is the slow part and BkB_{k} is the fast part of the generator, see (5.2) and (5.3). Since Aβn,k→Aα^,kA_{\beta_{n},k}\to A_{\hat{\alpha},k} as finite matrices, the slow–fast reduction used in Proposition 5.1 applies, with minor notational changes, also to this nn-dependent situation. The limiting effective generator 𝒢α^,k\mathscr{G}_{\hat{\alpha},k} is given by the same formula there.

If α^∈(0,∞)V\hat{\alpha}\in(0,\infty)^{V}, then the rest of the proof of Theorem 2.3 goes through without changes: the limiting quantities wk​(α^)w_{k}(\hat{\alpha}) and λk,m​(α^)\lambda_{k,m}(\hat{\alpha}) appearing in (5.12) and (5.25) are exactly those analyzed in Sections 5.2–5.4. Thus, strictly positive subsequential directions do not create any additional difficulty.

The only genuinely new case is when α^x=0\hat{\alpha}_{x}=0 for some x∈Vx\in V. Then, the limiting effective generator may acquire additional zero eigenvalues: sites with α^x=0\hat{\alpha}_{x}=0 may generate further transient states and, depending on the graph, may also disconnect irreducible components of the limiting effective dynamics. In particular, the effective gap at scale εn=(αn)max\varepsilon_{n}=(\alpha_{n})_{\rm max} may vanish, so that the relevant gaps may be of smaller order than εn\varepsilon_{n}. In such a case, the first-order slow–fast limit does not determine the ratio gapk​(αn)/gap2​(αn){\rm gap}_{k}(\alpha_{n})/{\rm gap}_{2}(\alpha_{n}); one would have to analyze the next non-vanishing scales of the coordinates of αn\alpha_{n}. Although one expects the same two-particle mechanism to arise also through this further multi-scale analysis, we do not pursue this extension here, and prefer to state Theorem 2.3 in the clean directional regime with α^∈(0,∞)V\hat{\alpha}\in(0,\infty)^{V} fixed.

6. Non-conservative SIP. Setting and main results

In this section, we attach particle reservoirs to some sites of the graph. We describe this by introducing two sets of non-negative site parameters, ω=(ωx)x∈V\omega=(\omega_{x})_{x\in V} and θ=(θx)x∈V\theta=(\theta_{x})_{x\in V}. The former one represents the rates of interaction between a site and its reservoir. The latter one prescribes the reservoirs’ particle densities. Next to the inclusion particles’ motion considered so far, we now let particles be created and annihilated with rates resembling those of SIP{\rm SIP}.

6.1. Model

Let G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) and α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V} be as in Section 2, and introduce some non-negative site weights ω=(ωx)x∈V\omega=(\omega_{x})_{x\in V} and θ=(θx)x∈V\theta=(\theta_{x})_{x\in V}. Then, we write SIP⁡(G,α,ω,θ){\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\theta) for the Markov process on22 2 Ξ0≔{∅}\Xi_{0}\coloneqq\{\emptyset\} consists of the empty configuration ∅\emptyset with no particles. Ξ≔∪k=0∞Ξk\Xi\coloneqq\cup_{k=0}^{\infty}\,\Xi_{k} with infinitesimal generator LG,α,ω,θL_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta} given, for a bounded function f∈ℝΞf\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi} and a configuration η∈Ξ\eta\in\Xi, by

(6.1) LG,α,ω,θ​f​(η)=∑x,y∈Vcx​y​ηx​(αy+ηy)​(f⁡(η−δx+δy)−f⁡(η))\displaystyle L_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta}f(\eta)=\sum_{x,y\in V}c_{xy}\,\eta_{x}\left(\alpha_{y}+\eta_{y}\right)\left(f(\eta-\delta_{x}+\delta_{y})-f(\eta)\right)
+∑x∈Vωx{ηx(1+θx)(f(η−δx)−f(η))+θx(αx+ηx)(f(η+δx)−f(η))}.\displaystyle+\sum_{x\in V}\omega_{x}\,\big\{\eta_{x}\left(1+\theta_{x}\right)\left(f(\eta-\delta_{x})-f(\eta)\right)+\theta_{x}\left(\alpha_{x}+\eta_{x}\right)\left(f(\eta+\delta_{x})-f(\eta)\right)\big\}\;\text{.}

Here, the first summation on the right-hand side corresponds with the conservative dynamics described by LG,α,kL_{G,\alpha,k} in (2.2), and is referred to as bulk dynamics. The second summation concerns the particle creation-annihilation mechanism, and may be interpreted as a bulk-boundary dynamics. More in detail, particles at x∈Vx\in V get killed independently, each at rate ωx​(1+θx)\omega_{x}\left(1+\theta_{x}\right), while a new particle is created at x∈Vx\in V with a configuration-dependent rate ωx​θx​(αx+ηx)\omega_{x}\,\theta_{x}\left(\alpha_{x}+\eta_{x}\right). Furthermore, albeit the configuration space Ξ\Xi is countably infinite, SIP⁡(G,α,ω,θ){\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\theta) does not explode in finite time. Indeed, the total number of particles is stochastically dominated by a pure birth process with linearly growing rates (see, e.g., [FGS22, Proposition 2.1]).

The long-time behavior of SIP⁡(G,α,ω,θ){\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\theta) clearly depends on the values of ω\omega and θ\theta. To start with, we mention that ωx=0\omega_{x}=0 means that site x∈Vx\in V does not directly exchange particles with any reservoirs, whereas θx=0\theta_{x}=0 corresponds to having a purely absorbing reservoir at x∈Vx\in V. As a consequence, if ω≡0\omega\equiv 0, we recover the conservative case having, for any total number of particles k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k} in (2.3) as a unique reversible measure. If θ≡0\theta\equiv 0 and ω≢0\omega\not\equiv 0, the system eventually empties out. In other words, if θ\theta vanishes on the support of ω\omega, that is,

(6.2) supp⁡(ω)≔{x∈V:ωx>0}​,{\rm supp}(\omega)\coloneqq\{x\in V:\omega_{x}>0\}\;\text{,}\;\;

then SIP⁡(G,α,ω,θ){\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\theta) has the empty configuration ∅∈Ξ0\emptyset\in\Xi_{0} as its unique stationary state, which, in turn, is absorbing. More generally, for ω≢0\omega\not\equiv 0, there exists a unique stationary measure for SIP⁡(G,α,ω,θ){\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\theta), referred to as μG,α,ω,θ\mu_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta}. In this situation, one typically distinguishes between two scenarios, commonly referred to as equilibrium and non-equilibrium, respectively.

More in detail, equilibrium occurs if θ\theta is constant on supp⁡(ω){\rm supp}(\omega). In this case, μG,α,ω,θ\mu_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta} is reversible, in product form, and explicit (see, e.g., [CGGR13, FRS22]): assuming that θ≡ϱ>0\theta\equiv\varrho>0, then μG,α,ω,θ=να,ϱ\mu_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta}=\nu_{\alpha,\varrho}, where, for all η∈Ξ\eta\in\Xi,

(6.3) να,ϱ​(η)≔1𝒵α,ϱ​(ϱ1+ϱ)|η|​∏x∈VΓ⁡(αx+ηx)Γ⁡(αx)​ηx!​,with​𝒵α,ϱ≔(1+ϱ)|α|​.\nu_{\alpha,\varrho}(\eta)\coloneqq\frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha,\varrho}}\left(\frac{\varrho}{1+\varrho}\right)^{|\eta|}\prod_{x\in V}\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_{x}+\eta_{x})}{\Gamma(\alpha_{x})\,\eta_{x}!}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\text{with}\ \mathcal{Z}_{\alpha,\varrho}\coloneqq(1+\varrho)^{|\alpha|}\;\text{.}

Note that μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k} in (2.3) is the canonical measure associated to the grand-canonical να,ϱ\nu_{\alpha,\varrho}. One speaks of non-equilibrium if θ\theta is non-constant on supp⁡(ω){\rm supp}(\omega). Then, μG,α,ω,θ\mu_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta} is, in general, neither reversible, nor in product form, nor explicit. We will not need to know more on the structure of this steady state; for further details, see, e.g., [FRS22] and references therein.

6.2. Spectral gap identity when θ≡0\theta\equiv 0

We start with the analysis of the purely absorbing SIP{\rm SIP}. As already anticipated in Section 1.4, we shall see that understanding the case θ≡0\theta\equiv 0 is one of the key ingredients for the spectral analysis of the setting with general θ\theta.

Observe that substituting θ≡0\theta\equiv 0 in (6.1) gives rise to a system in which all particles are never created, and get annihilated one at the time, until the system eventually gets empty. In particular, LG,α,ω,0L_{G,\alpha,\omega,0}, interpreted as an infinite matrix, is similar to a block lower triangular one. Moreover, the blocks on the diagonal — each for any total number of particles k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0} in the bulk of the system — are of finite size and describe the following finite-state Markov chains. The case k=1k=1 corresponds to a process with just one particle in the bulk, which moves as RW⁡(G,α){\rm RW}(G,\alpha) defined in Section 2, additionally killed at rate ωx≥0\omega_{x}\geq 0 when sitting on x∈Vx\in V. We refer to this process as RW⁡(G,α,ω){\rm RW}(G,\alpha,\omega). The case k≥2k\geq 2 is similar, with kk interacting particles evolving in the bulk as SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha), each independently killed with rate ωx≥0\omega_{x}\geq 0 when sitting at x∈Vx\in V. Each of these Markov chains, say SIPk​(G,α,ω){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha,\omega), is sub-stochastic. Moreover, since the conservative SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha) admits μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k} in (2.3) as its unique reversible measure, all eigenvalues of (the negative of) the generator of SIPk​(G,α,ω){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha,\omega) (see (7.1)) are real; as the conservative system is irreducible, supp⁡(ω)≠∅{\rm supp}(\omega)\neq\varnothing further ensures that such eigenvalues are strictly positive. Letting gapk​(G,α,ω){\rm gap}_{k}(G,\alpha,\omega), k≥1k\geq 1, be the lowest of such eigenvalues, we write (cf. (2.5))

(6.4) gapSIP​(G,α,ω)=infk≥1gapk​(G,α,ω)​.{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega)=\inf_{k\geq 1}{\rm gap}_{k}(G,\alpha,\omega)\;\text{.}

Similarly, we introduce the spectral gap of RW⁡(G,α,ω){\rm RW}(G,\alpha,\omega) as

(6.5) gapRW​(G,α,ω)=gap1​(G,α,ω)​.{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha,\omega)={\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha,\omega)\;\text{.}

Our main result of this section establishes that, as soon as the killing rate ω\omega is not identically zero, the spectral gaps in (6.4) and (6.5) coincide, regardless of the underlying geometry and of the site weights — even when αmin∈(0,1)\alpha_{\rm min}\in(0,1). This spectral gap identity stands in stark contrast to the behavior observed in the conservative setting, where restrictions are imposed on the value of αmin\alpha_{\rm min}.

Theorem 6.1 (θ≡0\theta\equiv 0).

For all graphs G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}), and site weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, ω=(ωx)x∈V\omega=(\omega_{x})_{x\in V} with ω≠0\omega\neq 0, we have

(6.6) gapSIP​(G,α,ω)=gapRW​(G,α,ω)​.{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega)={\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha,\omega)\;\text{.}

Remarkably, the proof of the above identity (deferred to Section 7.1) is quite elementary.

6.3. General setting

When dealing with the general case θ≠0\theta\neq 0, we must specify the infinite-dimensional function analytic setting that we work in. For this purpose, we define a class of functions on Ξ\Xi (Definition 6.2), written in terms of orthogonal “Meixner” polynomial dualities introduced in [FRS22, Section 4], which take the following form: for all ϱ≥0\varrho\geq 0,

Definition 6.2.

For all ϱ>0\varrho>0, integers k≥1k\geq 1, and functions ψ∈ℝΞk\psi\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}, define

(6.11) Fα,ϱψ​(η)≔∑ξ∈Ξkμα,k​(ξ)​ψ​(ξ)​Dα,ϱ​(ξ,η)​,η∈Ξ​.F_{\alpha,\varrho}^{\psi}(\eta)\coloneqq\sum_{\xi\in\Xi_{k}}\mu_{\alpha,k}(\xi)\,\psi(\xi)\,D_{\alpha,\varrho}(\xi,\eta)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\eta\in\Xi\;\text{.}

When k=0k=0 and, thus, ψ∈ℝ\psi\in\mathbb{R} is a scalar, we conventionally set Fα,ϱψ≡ψ∈ℝF_{\alpha,\varrho}^{\psi}\equiv\psi\in\mathbb{R}.

Remark that, as long as ψ≠0\psi\neq 0, the function in (6.11) is a non-vanishing kk-th order polynomial in the variables η=(ηx)x∈V\eta=(\eta_{x})_{x\in V}. In particular, expressions like LG,α,ω,θ​Fα,ϱψL_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta}F_{\alpha,\varrho}^{\psi} will always be well defined. Finally, introduce the operators 𝔟α,ω,ϱ,k−1θ:ℝΞk→ℝΞk−1\mathfrak{b}_{\alpha,\omega,\varrho,k-1}^{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}}, k≥1k\geq 1, acting on functions ψ∈ℝΞk\psi\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} as

(6.12) 𝔟α,ω,ϱ,k−1θ​ψ​(ζ)≔k​∑x∈Vωx​(θx−ϱ)​αx+ζx|α|+k−1​ψ​(ζ+δx)​,ζ∈Ξk−1​.\mathfrak{b}_{\alpha,\omega,\varrho,k-1}^{\theta}\psi(\zeta)\coloneqq k\sum_{x\in V}\omega_{x}\left(\theta_{x}-\varrho\right)\frac{\alpha_{x}+\zeta_{x}}{|\alpha|+k-1}\,\psi(\zeta+\delta_{x})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\zeta\in\Xi_{k-1}\;\text{.}

Clearly, we have

(6.13) 𝔟α,ω,ϱ,k−1θ=0​,if​θ≡ϱ​.\mathfrak{b}_{\alpha,\omega,\varrho,k-1}^{\theta}=0\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\text{if}\ \theta\equiv\varrho\;\text{.}

The following theorem, whose proof is postponed to Section 7.2 below, is stated for any graph GG and site weights α\alpha, ω\omega, and θ\theta.

Theorem 6.3.

Fix ϱ>0\varrho>0 and recall Definition 6.2.

  1. (1)

    Given k≥0k\geq 0, any eigenpair λ,ψ\lambda,\psi of the kk-particle purely-absorbing system solves

    (6.14) LG,α,ω,θ​Fα,ϱψ=−λ​Fα,ϱψ+Fα,ϱ𝔟α,ω,ϱ,k−1θ​ψ​.L_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta}F_{\alpha,\varrho}^{\psi}=-\lambda\,F_{\alpha,\varrho}^{\psi}+F_{\alpha,\varrho}^{\mathfrak{b}_{\alpha,\omega,\varrho,k-1}^{\theta}\psi}\;\text{.}
  2. (2)

    The functions Fα,ϱψF_{\alpha,\varrho}^{\psi} as in Definition 6.2 may be chosen to form an orthogonal basis of L2​(να,ϱ)L^{2}(\nu_{\alpha,\varrho}).

Let us comment on two powerful consequences of the above theorem in the reversible case θ≡ϱ\theta\equiv\varrho (we discuss the non-reversible case in Remark 6.5 below; see also Remark 6.6 for a comparison with the symmetric exclusion process). The first item tells us that any eigenvalue of the purely absorbing system with k≥1k\geq 1 particles is one also for the general system and, moreover, it provides a constructive procedure to build eigenfunctions from those of the kk-particle absorbing system. Indeed, by (6.13), the identity in (6.14) becomes the eigenvalue equation

(6.15) LG,α,ω,θ​Fα,ϱψ=−λ​Fα,ϱψ​,L_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta}F_{\alpha,\varrho}^{\psi}=-\lambda\,F_{\alpha,\varrho}^{\psi}\;\text{,}\;\;

because the second term on the right-hand side of (6.14) vanishes when θ≡ϱ\theta\equiv\varrho. The second item guarantees the existence of a complete orthonormal system of eigenfunctions of LG,α,ω,θL_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta}. This, combined with the fact that the generator is self-adjoint in the associated L2L^{2}-space, ensures that −LG,α,ω,θ-L_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta} has a pure point spectrum therein, all contained in [0,∞)[0,\infty), with a gap after the zero eigenvalue coinciding with that of the purely absorbing system. Letting

(6.16) gapSIP​(G,α,ω,ϱ){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\varrho)

denote this spectral gap when θ≡ϱ>0\theta\equiv\varrho>0, Theorem 6.1 readily implies the following result.

Corollary 6.4 (θ≡ϱ\theta\equiv\varrho).

For all graphs G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}), and site weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, ω=(ωx)x∈V\omega=(\omega_{x})_{x\in V} with ω≠0\omega\neq 0, we have

(6.17) gapSIP​(G,α,ω,ϱ)=gapRW​(G,α,ω)​,ϱ>0​.{\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\varrho)={\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha,\omega)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\varrho>0\;\text{.}

The above result is stated in the reversible setting θ≡ϱ\theta\equiv\varrho. The next two remarks clarify the corresponding non-reversible picture: for the infinite-state SIP\mathrm{SIP} one has to distinguish algebraic eigenfunction lifting from a full spectral statement on a prescribed function space (Remark 6.5), whereas in finite-state analogues such as the partial symmetric exclusion process this distinction disappears (Remark 6.6).

Remark 6.5 (Non-reversible setting).

In view of Theorem 6.3, it is plausible to expect that Corollary 6.4 should extend, in some sense, to the non-reversible setting as well. Indeed, since the two functions on the right-hand side of (6.14) are polynomials of order kk and ℓ≤k−1\ell\leq k-1, this guarantees that λ\lambda therein lies in the point spectrum of LG,α,ω,θL_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta}, for all θ=(θx)x∈V\theta=(\theta_{x})_{x\in V}. However, in absence of a natural Hilbert space ensuring that such eigenfunctions form a complete orthonormal system when θ≢const.\theta\not\equiv{\rm const.} on supp⁡(ω){\rm supp}(\omega), the presence, e.g., of a continuous part of the spectrum (a property which also depends on the choice of the underlying reference function space) is what Theorem 6.3 does not exclude.

Remark 6.6 (Symmetric exclusion processes & Co.).

The proof of Theorem 6.31 — based on orthogonal-polynomial dualities, annihilation and creation operators — carries over to other non-equilibrium systems enjoying similar properties, e.g., [RS18, FRS22, GRT25]. As an example, we mention the symmetric (partial) exclusion process (SEP{\rm SEP}) in contact with reservoirs (see, e.g., [FRS22, Sal23, Sal24]), whose generator is readily obtained from LG,α,ω,θL_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta} in (6.1) by further imposing α=(αx)x∈V⊂ℕ\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}\subset\mathbb{N} and θ=(θx)x∈V∈[0,1]\theta=(\theta_{x})_{x\in V}\in[0,1], and changing the plus signs in αx+ηx\alpha_{x}+\eta_{x} and 1+θx1+\theta_{x} therein into minus signs. In this case, the configuration space is simply ∏x∈V{0,1,…,αx}\prod_{x\in V}\{0,1,\ldots,\alpha_{x}\}, thus finite, and the technical issues explained in Remark 6.5 do not arise: the spectrum is just the union of finitely many eigenvalues.

As our proof arguments used for SIP{\rm SIP} adapt to the open SEP{\rm SEP}, one obtains analogues of Theorems 6.1 and 6.3: on the one hand, the eigenvalues of the open SEP{\rm SEP} with arbitrary reservoir densities θ∈[0,1]V\theta\in[0,1]^{V} coincide with those of the purely absorbing case θ≡0\theta\equiv 0, and are therefore independent of θ\theta; on the other hand, importing the notation used above, one has gapSEP​(G,α,ω)=gapRW​(G,α,ω){\rm gap}_{\rm SEP}(G,\alpha,\omega)={\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha,\omega). These two results further ensure that

(6.18) gapSEP​(G,α,ω,θ)=gapRW​(G,α,ω)​,θ∈[0,1]V​.{\rm gap}_{\rm SEP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\theta)={\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha,\omega)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\theta\in[0,1]^{V}\;\text{.}

This, thus, recovers, in the reversible case, the spectral-gap identity of [Sal23, Corollary 1], and, for general reservoir densities, the corresponding result of [Sal24, Theorem 2].

7. Proofs of Theorems 6.1 and 6.3

The following two sections may be essentially read independently.

7.1. Proof of Theorem 6.1

For every k≥1k\geq 1, the kk-particle purely absorbing system (i.e., when θ≡0\theta\equiv 0) is described by the infinitesimal generator

(7.1) LG,α,ω,k​f​(η)≔LG,α,k​f​(η)−f⁡(η)​∑x∈Vωx​ηx​,L_{G,\alpha,\omega,k}f(\eta)\coloneqq L_{G,\alpha,k}f(\eta)-f(\eta)\sum_{x\in V}\omega_{x}\,\eta_{x}\;\text{,}\;\;

Equivalently, if f∈ℝΞkf\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} is extended to Ξ\Xi by setting f≡0f\equiv 0 on Ξ∖Ξk\Xi\setminus\Xi_{k}, then the restriction to Ξk\Xi_{k} of the generator in (6.1) with θ≡0\theta\equiv 0 is precisely the operator in (7.1). Note that, when the process is in configuration η∈Ξk\eta\in\Xi_{k}, it gets killed with rate ∑x∈Vωx​ηx≥0\sum_{x\in V}\omega_{x}\,\eta_{x}\geq 0.

Recall the definition of the probability measure μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k} in (2.3). Since LG,α,ω,kL_{G,\alpha,\omega,k} is the sum of a self-adjoint operator on L2​(μα,k)L^{2}(\mu_{\alpha,k}) and a multiplicative one, it is self-adjoint on L2​(μα,k)L^{2}(\mu_{\alpha,k}) and, thus, all the eigenvalues of −LG,α,ω,k-L_{G,\alpha,\omega,k} are real and non-negative. Additionally, since the conservative dynamics is irreducible and the multiplication operator is non-positive, all such eigenvalues are actually strictly positive. In particular, we obtain that gapk​(G,α,ω){\rm gap}_{k}(G,\alpha,\omega), the lowest of such eigenvalues, is positive and, by the Perron-Frobenius theorem, characterized as the worst-case exponential killing rate for large times: letting τk\tau_{k} denote the first time at which one of the kk particles gets killed,

(7.2) gapk(G,α,ω)=−limt→∞1tlogmaxη∈ΞkℙηG,α,ω,k[τk>t].{\rm gap}_{k}(G,\alpha,\omega)=-\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{t}\log\max_{\eta\in\Xi_{k}}\mathds{P}_{\eta}^{G,\alpha,\omega,k}[\tau_{k}>t]\;\text{.}

Thanks to this asymptotic identity, the assertion of Theorem 6.1 boils down to show that, for all k≥2k\geq 2,

(7.3) maxη∈ΞkℙηG,α,ω,k[τk>t]≤maxx∈VℙδxG,α,ω,1[τ1>t],t≥0.\max_{\eta\in\Xi_{k}}\mathds{P}_{\eta}^{G,\alpha,\omega,k}[\tau_{k}>t]\leq\max_{x\in V}\mathds{P}_{\delta_{x}}^{G,\alpha,\omega,1}[\tau_{1}>t]\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad t\geq 0\;\text{.}

For this purpose, we introduce a lookdown representation of the particle system with killing, extending the one known within the conservative setting [KS24, Appendix A]. We need to introduce a bit of notation. For every k≥2k\geq 2, labeled configuration 𝐱=(x1,…,xk)∈Vk\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\in V^{k}, and permutation ς∈Sk\varsigma\in S_{k}, we write ς​𝐱=(xς⁡(1),…,xς⁡(k))∈Vk\varsigma\mathbf{x}=(x_{\varsigma(1)},\ldots,x_{\varsigma(k)})\in V^{k}. Further, 𝒮k:ℝVk→ℝVk\mathcal{S}_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{V^{k}}\to\mathbb{R}^{V^{k}} denotes the symmetrization operator, that is,

(7.4) 𝒮k​φ​(𝐱)=1k!​∑ς∈Skφ⁡(ς​𝐱)​,φ∈ℝVk​,\mathcal{S}_{k}\varphi(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{\varsigma\in S_{k}}\varphi(\varsigma\mathbf{x})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\varphi\in\mathbb{R}^{V^{k}}\;\text{,}\;\;

7.2. Proof of Theorem 6.3

Our main ingredient will be the duality property of SIP{\rm SIP} in contact with reservoirs (e.g., [GKRV09, CGGR13]), in particular, the orthogonal polynomial duality functions found in [FRS22]. We shall not assume any prior knowledge on this topic, but rather exploit a few properties taken from [KLS10, RS18, FRS22], which, for the reader’s convenience, we collect in the following proposition. For notational convenience, we simply write Lθ=LG,α,ω,θL_{\theta}=L_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta} and Lk=LG,α,ω,kL_{k}=L_{G,\alpha,\omega,k} (defined in (6.1) and (7.1), respectively).

Proposition 7.2.

Fix ϱ>0\varrho>0.

    Orthogonality and completeness. Let ⟨⋅|⋅⟩α,ϱ\left\langle\,\cdot\,\,\middle|\,\,\cdot\,\right\rangle_{\alpha,\varrho} denote the inner product in L2​(να,ϱ)L^{2}(\nu_{\alpha,\varrho}) (see (6.3)). Then, for all integers k,ℓ≥1k,\ell\geq 1 and ξ∈Ξk\xi\in\Xi_{k}, ζ∈Ξℓ\zeta\in\Xi_{\ell},

    (7.11) ⟨Dα,ϱ​(ξ,⋅)|Dα,ϱ​(ζ,⋅)⟩α,ϱ=𝟙{ξ=ζ}ϱk​(1+ϱ)kZα,kμα,k(ξ)−1​.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \left\langle D_{\alpha,\varrho}(\xi,\,\cdot\,)\,\middle|\,D_{\alpha,\varrho}(\zeta,\,\cdot\,)\right\rangle_{\alpha,\varrho}&={\mathds{1}_{\{\xi=\zeta\}}}\,\frac{\varrho^{k}\left(1+\varrho\right)^{k}}{Z_{\alpha,k}}\,{\mu_{\alpha,k}(\xi)^{-1}}\end{aligned}\;\text{.}

    Moreover, {Dα,ϱ​(ξ,⋅)}k≥0,ξ∈Ξk\left\{D_{\alpha,\varrho}(\xi,\,\cdot\,)\right\}_{k\geq 0,\,\xi\in\Xi_{k}} is a complete system of L2​(να,ϱ)L^{2}(\nu_{\alpha,\varrho}).

  2. (2)

    Duality. For all θ=(θx)x∈V\theta=(\theta_{x})_{x\in V} and η∈Ξ\eta\in\Xi, we have

    (7.12) Lθ​Dα,ϱ​(ξ,⋅)​(η)=Lk​Dα,ϱ​(⋅,η)​(ξ)+∑x∈Vωxξx(θx−ϱ)Dα,ϱ(ξ−δx,η).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} L_{\theta}D_{\alpha,\varrho}(\xi,\,\cdot\,)(\eta)&=L_{k}D_{\alpha,\varrho}(\,\cdot\,,\eta)(\xi)\\ &+\sum_{x\in V}\omega_{x}\,\xi_{x}\left(\theta_{x}-\varrho\right)D_{\alpha,\varrho}(\xi-\delta_{x},\eta)\;\text{.}\end{aligned}
Remark 7.3.

Since {Dα,ϱ​(ξ,⋅)}ℓ≤k,ξ∈Ξℓ\left\{D_{\alpha,\varrho}(\xi,\,\cdot\,)\right\}_{\ell\leq k,\,\xi\in\Xi_{\ell}} spans all polynomials of order ≤k\leq k, by (7.12), Lθ=LG,α,ω,θL_{\theta}=L_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta} leaves invariant such a subspace of polynomials.

Proof of Theorem 6.3.

The rest of the proof of Theorem 6.3 is routine. Indeed, Theorem 6.31 follows by linearity and the duality relation in (7.12): recalling Fα,ϱψF_{\alpha,\varrho}^{\psi} from Definition 6.2, first we obtain

which, by (3.12) and the definition of 𝔟α,ω,ϱ,k−1ϱ\mathfrak{b}_{\alpha,\omega,\varrho,k-1}^{\varrho} in (6.12), rearranges as
