for some constant 𝔠α,ϱ,k>0\mathfrak{c}_{\alpha,\varrho,k}>0.

The completeness of the functions in (6.10) follows from a one-dimensional density result. Each marginal of να,ϱ\nu_{\alpha,\varrho} is a negative-binomial measure, hence has exponential tails and a determinate Hamburger moment problem. By the classical theorem of M. Riesz [Rie24] (see also [Akh65, Chapter 2, Section 3 and Corollary 2.3.3], [BC81, Ber96], and references therein), determinacy implies density of algebraic polynomials in the corresponding L2L^{2}-space. Since VV is finite and να,ϱ\nu_{\alpha,\varrho} is a product measure on ℕ0V\mathbb{N}_{0}^{V}, tensor products of these univariate polynomial bases are dense in L2​(να,ϱ)L^{2}(\nu_{\alpha,\varrho}), yielding the desired completeness. ∎

8. Extensions and related models

In this last section, we extend our results to the Brownian energy process, and briefly discuss their connections with what is known for some closely related models.

8.1. Brownian energy process

Given a graph G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) and site weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, the corresponding Brownian energy process — referred to as BEP⁡(G,α){\rm BEP}(G,\alpha) — is the diffusion on the probability simplex

(8.1) Σ≔{ζ∈[0,1]V:∑x∈Vζx=1}​,\varSigma\coloneqq\left\{\zeta\in[0,1]^{V}:\sum_{x\in V}\zeta_{x}=1\right\}\;\text{,}\;\;

with infinitesimal generator

(8.2) ℒG,α=12∑x,y∈Vcx​y{−(αyζx−αxζy)(∂ζx−∂ζy)+ζxζy(∂ζx−∂ζy)2},\mathcal{L}_{G,\alpha}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x,y\in V}c_{xy}\left\{-\left(\alpha_{y}\zeta_{x}-\alpha_{x}\zeta_{y}\right)\left(\partial_{\zeta_{x}}-\partial_{\zeta_{y}}\right)+\zeta_{x}\zeta_{y}\left(\partial_{\zeta_{x}}-\partial_{\zeta_{y}}\right)^{2}\right\}\;\text{,}\;\;

and the following Dirichlet distribution on Σ\varSigma as its unique reversible measure

(8.3) γα​(d​ζ)=(1B⁡(α)​∏x∈Vζxαx−1)​d​ζ​,with​B​(α)≔∏x∈VΓ⁡(αx)Γ⁡(|α|)​.\gamma_{\alpha}({\rm d}\zeta)=\left(\frac{1}{{\rm B}(\alpha)}\prod_{x\in V}\zeta_{x}^{\alpha_{x}-1}\right){\rm d}\zeta\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\text{with}\ {\rm B}(\alpha)\coloneqq\frac{\prod_{x\in V}\Gamma(\alpha_{x})}{\Gamma(|\alpha|)}\;\text{.}

Here, d​ζ{\rm d}\zeta stands for the uniform measure on Σ\varSigma. We refer to Section 1, [KS24] and references therein, for more information and history on this model. Here, we just mention that its mean field version (i.e., when cx​y≡const.c_{xy}\equiv{\rm const.}) coincides with the renowned multi-type Wright-Fisher diffusion with parent independent mutations (see, e.g., [Shi77, WZ19]).

As shown in [KS24], BEP⁡(G,α){\rm BEP}(G,\alpha) inherits its eigenstructure from that of SIP⁡(G,α){\rm SIP}(G,\alpha). More precisely, the Poisson intertwining relation [KS24, Eq. (4.1)] between the generators ℒG,α\mathcal{L}_{G,\alpha} and LG,α,kL_{G,\alpha,k} allows to lift eigenfunctions of SIP⁡(G,α){\rm SIP}(G,\alpha) to eigenfunctions of BEP⁡(G,α){\rm BEP}(G,\alpha), both corresponding to the same eigenvalue. Using this intertwining relation (and, more specifically, that ℒG,α\mathcal{L}_{G,\alpha} maps the finite-dimensional subspace of polynomials of degree at most kk into itself) and the fact ℒG,α\mathcal{L}_{G,\alpha} is a self-adjoint operator on L2​(γα)L^{2}(\gamma_{\alpha}), one concludes that this lifting saturates all the spectral information (i.e., the spectrum of BEP{\rm BEP} is pure point and coincides with that of SIP{\rm SIP}; see [KS24, Sections 1.2 and 4] for further details). In particular, the corresponding spectral gaps coincide

(8.4) gapBEP​(G,α)=gapSIP​(G,α)​.{\rm gap}_{\rm BEP}(G,\alpha)={\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)\;\text{.}

Combining the findings in [KS24] with our Theorems 2.2 and 2.4 on gapSIP​(G,α){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha), we readily deduce the following analogues of (1.4) and (1.8).

Corollary 8.1.

For all graphs G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) and site weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, we have

(8.5) αmin​{121​αratio6αmin/αratio​cmin|V|2​diam​(G)}≤gapBEP​(G,α)≤gapRW​(G,α)​,\alpha_{\rm min}\left\{\frac{1}{21}\,\frac{\alpha_{\rm ratio}}{6^{\alpha_{\rm min}/\alpha_{\rm ratio}}}\,\frac{c_{\rm min}}{|V|^{2}\,{\rm diam}(G)}\right\}\leq{\rm gap}_{\rm BEP}(G,\alpha)\leq{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)\;\text{,}\;\;

and, in some cases, we have

(8.6) gapBEP​(G,α)<gapRW​(G,α)​.{\rm gap}_{\rm BEP}(G,\alpha)<{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)\;\text{.}

Interestingly, also our results on the spectrum of the non-conservative SIP{\rm SIP}, via similar arguments, translate to the context of the BEP{\rm BEP}. Indeed, the aforementioned Poisson intertwining is effective also when one adds the interaction with external reservoirs. As shown, e.g., in [GRT25, Section 4.1], using this operator, the generator LG,α,ω,θL_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta} in (6.1) of SIP⁡(G,α,ω,θ){\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\theta) satisfies, for all ω=(ωx)x∈V\omega=(\omega_{x})_{x\in V} and θ=(θx)x∈V\theta=(\theta_{x})_{x\in V}, an analogous intertwining relation with

(8.7) ℒG,α,ω,θ=ℒG,α+∑x∈Vωx{(αxθx−ζx)∂ζx+θxζx∂ζx2},\mathcal{L}_{G,\alpha,\omega,\theta}=\mathcal{L}_{G,\alpha}+\sum_{x\in V}\omega_{x}\left\{\left(\alpha_{x}\theta_{x}-\zeta_{x}\right)\partial_{\zeta_{x}}+\theta_{x}\zeta_{x}\,\partial_{\zeta_{x}}^{2}\right\}\;\text{,}\;\;

the generator of what we refer to as BEP⁡(G,α,ω,θ){\rm BEP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\theta).

When θ≡ϱ>0\theta\equiv\varrho>0, this non-conservative diffusion on [0,∞)V[0,\infty)^{V} is well known to have the following product measure γα,ϱ=⊗x∈VGamma(αx,ϱ)\gamma_{\alpha,\varrho}=\otimes_{x\in V}\,{\rm Gamma}(\alpha_{x},\varrho) as its unique reversible measure. Hence, arguing as above, we derive the corresponding spectral gap identity

(8.8) gapBEP​(G,α,ω,ϱ)=gapSIP​(G,α,ω,ϱ)​,{\rm gap}_{\rm BEP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\varrho)={\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\varrho)\;\text{,}\;\;

and, as a consequence, the following analogue of Corollary 6.4.

Corollary 8.2.

For all graphs G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}), and site weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, ω=(ωx)x∈V\omega=(\omega_{x})_{x\in V} with ω≠0\omega\neq 0, we have

(8.9) gapBEP​(G,α,ω,ϱ)=gapRW​(G,α,ω)​,ϱ>0​,{\rm gap}_{\rm BEP}(G,\alpha,\omega,\varrho)={\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha,\omega)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\varrho>0\;\text{,}\;\;

where gapRW​(G,α,ω){\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha,\omega) is defined in (6.5).

8.2. Other models

As already anticipated in Section 1, SIP{\rm SIP} and BEP{\rm BEP} come with several closely related models, having a different dynamics, but exactly the same steady states. The models we have in mind fall into the class of mass redistribution models. Here, we shall focus only on those models with configuration-independent edge updates (see, e.g., [Sas15] and references therein for configuration-dependent mass redistribution models with Dirichlet-type steady states): after an edge, say x​yxy, is selected with rate cx​y≥0c_{xy}\geq 0, particles/energies sitting on xx and yy get randomly redistributed therein. Among them, let us mention:

  1. (1)

    the Beta-Binomial splitting process and its continuous version, also known as Beta splitting process or (generalized) KMP model (see, e.g., [PR26, DMFG24, GRT25]);

  2. (2)

    the discrete and continuous harmonic processes (see, e.g., [FFG23, GRT25]).

All models in (a) and (b) have been studied in their conservative and non-conservative variants (see the aforementioned references for the precise definitions of the redistribution rules), and, just like SIP{\rm SIP} and BEP{\rm BEP}, discrete and corresponding continuous models are isospectral (when reversible), enjoying completely analogous Poisson intertwining relations.

To the best of our knowledge, the only sharp quantitative results on their convergence to equilibrium are confined to a handful of results, see [CCL03, Smi14, CLL20, PR26] and references therein. For what concerns the spectral gap, the only sharp results that we are aware of concern the Beta and Beta-Binomial splitting processes in two specific settings, both conservative:

  1. (1)

    the complete graph with α≡const.\alpha\equiv{\rm const.} [CCL03] (see also [CLL20, Remark 4]);

  2. (2)

    the segment with α≡const.≥1\alpha\equiv{\rm const.}\geq 1 [CLL20].

In particular, in (i), the gap is attained by the system with k=2k=2 particles (which is strictly smaller than gap1{\rm gap}_{1}), while in (ii) it coincides with that of the corresponding single particle.

In order to obtain spectral gap asymptotics for small diffusivity, the proof ideas of Theorems 2.3 and 2.4 apply also to these models (actually, with considerable simplifications due to the presence of edge updates only, and edges are a.s. never updated simultaneously). For instance, it is not difficult to show that, on graphs like that in Section 5.5 and for α\alpha small enough, the spectral gap of the two particles must be strictly smaller than that of the single random walk. Similarly, the non-conservative (reversible) models satisfy a one-particle spectral gap identity, analogous to the one contained in Corollary 6.4. Indeed, the key step in that proof (Section 7.1) carries over to these other models in contact with reservoirs, because of the analogous intertwining and consistency/duality relations available also for them, see, e.g., [GRT25]. We leave the verification of these claims to the interested reader. What remains largely open is the problem of obtaining spectral gap’s sharp lower bounds — and, possibly, identities in terms of simpler processes — for the conservative variants of these mass redistribution models on general geometries.

Hence, each of the random variables τ1,τ2−τ1′,…,τm+1−τm′\tau_{1},\tau_{2}-\tau_{1}^{\prime},\dots,\tau_{m+1}-\tau_{m}^{\prime} stochastically dominates an exponential random variable with rate cmax​k​α^maxc_{\rm max}\,k\,\hat{\alpha}_{\rm max}. Thus, letting τ1∗,τ2∗,…\tau_{1}^{*},\tau_{2}^{*},\dots be some i.i.d. exponentials of rate cmax​k​α^maxc_{\rm max}\,k\,\hat{\alpha}_{\rm max}, by Markovianity we get

(A.28) ℙηε[τm+1≤t+δ]\displaystyle\mathds{P}_{\eta}^{\varepsilon}\,[\tau_{m+1}\leq t+\delta] ≤ℙ[τ1∗+⋯+τm+1∗≤t+δ]\displaystyle\leq\mathds{P}\,[\tau_{1}^{*}+\cdots+\tau_{m+1}^{*}\leq t+\delta]
=ℙ[Gamma(m+1,cmaxkα^max)≤t+δ]→m→∞0,\displaystyle=\mathds{P}\,[{\rm Gamma}\,(m+1,c_{\rm max}\,k\,\hat{\alpha}_{\rm max})\leq t+\delta]\xrightarrow{m\to\infty}0\;\text{,}\;\;

where Gamma⁡(u,β){\rm Gamma}\,(u,\beta) denotes the Gamma distribution with shape u>0u>0 and rate β>0\beta>0. Therefore, by (A.23), (A.26) and (A.28), we conclude that

(A.29) lim supε→0ℙηε[Tε(t+δ)≤t]\displaystyle\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}\mathds{P}_{\eta}^{\varepsilon}\,[T_{\varepsilon}(t+\delta)\leq t] ≤lim supm→∞lim supε→0m2​C1​ε​log⁡kδ​cmin\displaystyle\leq\limsup_{m\to\infty}\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{m^{2}\,{C_{1}}\,\varepsilon\,\log k}{\delta\,c_{\rm min}}
(A.30) +lim supm→∞ℙ[Gamma(m+1,cmaxkα^max)≤t+δ]=0,\displaystyle+\limsup_{m\to\infty}\mathds{P}\,[{\rm Gamma}\,(m+1,c_{\rm max}\,k\,\hat{\alpha}_{\rm max})\leq t+\delta]=0\;\text{,}\;\;

as desired. ∎

Lemma A.4.

We have

(A.31) limδ→0limε→0supξ∈Ωkℙξε[τΔk<3δ]=0.\lim_{\delta\to 0}\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\sup_{\xi\in\Omega_{k}}\mathds{P}_{\xi}^{\varepsilon}\,[\tau_{\Delta_{k}}<3\delta]=0\;\text{.}
Proof.

As explained in the proof of Lemma A.3, starting from any ξ∈Ωk\xi\in\Omega_{k}, τΔk\tau_{\Delta_{k}} stochastically dominates an exponential random variable of rate cmax​k​α^maxc_{\rm max}\,k\,\hat{\alpha}_{\rm max}. Thus, we get

(A.32) lim supδ→0supε∈(0,1)ℙξε[τΔk<3δ]≤lim supδ→0(1−e−cmax​k​α^max​ 3​δ)=0.\limsup_{\delta\to 0}\sup_{\varepsilon\in(0,1)}\mathds{P}_{\xi}^{\varepsilon}\,[\tau_{\Delta_{k}}<3\delta]\leq\limsup_{\delta\to 0}\left(1-e^{-c_{\rm max}\,k\,\hat{\alpha}_{\rm max}\,3\delta}\right)=0\;\text{.}

This concludes the proof. ∎

Now, we are ready to prove Proposition A.1.

Proof of Proposition A.1.

We prove

(A.33) limε→0ℙηε[ηε(t)∈Ωk]=1,t>0,η∈Ξk.\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\mathds{P}_{\eta}^{\varepsilon}\,[\eta^{\varepsilon}(t)\in\Omega_{k}]=1\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad t>0\;\text{,}\;\;\eta\in\Xi_{k}\;\text{.}

We follow the proof ideas of [LLM18, Lemma 3.1]. By (A.16), for δ∈(0,t/3)\delta\in(0,t/3), we estimate

(A.34) 1=ℙηε[ηε(Sε(t−3δ))∈Ωk]≤\displaystyle 1=\mathds{P}_{\eta}^{\varepsilon}\,[\eta^{\varepsilon}(S_{\varepsilon}(t-3\delta))\in\Omega_{k}]\leq ℙηε​[ηε​(Sε​(t−3​δ))∈Ωk,Sε​(t−3​δ)∈[t−3​δ,t−2​δ]]\displaystyle\ \mathds{P}_{\eta}^{\varepsilon}\left[\eta^{\varepsilon}(S_{\varepsilon}(t-3\delta))\in\Omega_{k},\ S_{\varepsilon}(t-3\delta)\in[t-3\delta,t-2\delta]\right]
(A.35) +ℙηε[Sε(t−3δ)>t−2δ].\displaystyle+\mathds{P}_{\eta}^{\varepsilon}\,[S_{\varepsilon}(t-3\delta)>t-2\delta]\;\text{.}

By Lemma A.3, the second probability in the right-hand side vanishes as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. Moreover, by (A.16), the first probability in the right-hand side is bounded by

(A.36) ℙηε[∃s∈[t−3δ,t−2δ],ηε(s)∈Ωk].\mathds{P}_{\eta}^{\varepsilon}\,[\,\exists s\in[t-3\delta,t-2\delta],\ \eta^{\varepsilon}(s)\in\Omega_{k}\,]\;\text{.}

We can further divide this into two events and bound the last probability as

(A.37) ℙηε[ηε(t)∈Ωk]+ℙηε[∃s∈[t−3δ,t−2δ],ηε(s)∈Ωk,ηε(t)∈Δk].\mathds{P}_{\eta}^{\varepsilon}\,[\eta^{\varepsilon}(t)\in\Omega_{k}]+\mathds{P}_{\eta}^{\varepsilon}\,[\,\exists s\in[t-3\delta,t-2\delta],\ \eta^{\varepsilon}(s)\in\Omega_{k},\ \eta^{\varepsilon}(t)\in\Delta_{k}\,]\;\text{.}

Then, by the Markov property, the second probability above is bounded by

(A.38) supξ∈Ωkℙξε[τΔk<3δ],\sup_{\xi\in\Omega_{k}}\mathds{P}_{\xi}^{\varepsilon}\,[\tau_{\Delta_{k}}<3\delta]\;\text{,}\;\;

which, by Lemma A.4, vanishes by first taking the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, and then δ→0\delta\to 0. Collecting all displayed inequalities, we conclude that (A.33) holds. ∎

Appendix B Reversibility of the limit process

In this appendix, we prove Lemma 5.9 and simply write ςα^,k=ςα^,k,m\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k}=\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k,m}, k≥mk\geq m.

Proof of Lemma 5.9.

We start by introducing an auxiliary continuous-time Markov chain on Ξk\Xi_{k} with rate function (cf. (5.1)–(5.5))

(B.1) 𝐬⁡(η,⋅)≔{𝐫α^,k𝒜​(η,⋅)if​η∈Ωk​,𝐫kℬ​(η,⋅)if​η∈Δk​.{\bf s}(\eta,\,\cdot\,)\coloneqq\begin{cases}{\bf r}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\eta,\,\cdot\,)&\text{if}\ \eta\in\Omega_{k}\;\text{,}\\ {\bf r}^{\mathcal{B}}_{k}(\eta,\,\cdot\,)&\text{if}\ \eta\in\Delta_{k}\;\text{.}\end{cases}

In words, the above dynamics follows the rule of Aα^,kA_{\hat{\alpha},k} in Ωk\Omega_{k}, while that of BkB_{k} in Δk\Delta_{k}. (Remark that this is not a SIP{\rm SIP}-dynamics.) Now, recall the definition of Ωk,m\Omega_{k,m} from (5.17) and, similarly, introduce the set

(B.2) Δk,m≔{ζ∈Δk:|{x∈V:ζx>0}|=m}​.\Delta_{k,m}\coloneqq\left\{\zeta\in\Delta_{k}:|\{x\in V:\zeta_{x}>0\}|=m\right\}\;\text{.}

Observe that this auxiliary chain can jump from Ωk,m\Omega_{k,m} to either Δk,m\Delta_{k,m} or Δk,m+1\Delta_{k,m+1} (if m≤k−1m\leq k-1), but a jump from Ωk,m\Omega_{k,m} to Δk,m\Delta_{k,m} has rate zero to backtrack.

Now, fix m≤k−1m\leq k-1. We claim that this dynamics, restricted to Ωk,m∪Δk,m+1\Omega_{k,m}\cup\Delta_{k,m+1}, is reversible with respect to ςα^,k\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k}. For this purpose, it suffices to consider pairs η,ξ=η−δx+δy∈Ωk,m∪Δk,m+1\eta,\xi=\eta-\delta_{x}+\delta_{y}\in\Omega_{k,m}\cup\Delta_{k,m+1} (hence, ηx≥1\eta_{x}\geq 1); rates are zero otherwise. If η∈Ωk,m\eta\in\Omega_{k,m} and ξ∈Ωk,m\xi\in\Omega_{k,m} (such that ηx=1\eta_{x}=1), then

(B.3) ςα^,k​(η)​𝐫α^,k𝒜​(η,ξ)=cx​y​ηx​α^y​∏z∈Vηz>0α^zηz=cx​y​α^x​ξy​∏z∈Vξz>0α^zξz=ςα^,k​(ξ)​𝐫α^,k𝒜​(ξ,η)​.\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\eta)\,{\bf r}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\eta,\xi)=c_{xy}\,\eta_{x}\hat{\alpha}_{y}\,\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in V\\ \eta_{z}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{\hat{\alpha}_{z}}{\eta_{z}}=c_{xy}\,\hat{\alpha}_{x}\xi_{y}\,\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in V\\ \xi_{z}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{\hat{\alpha}_{z}}{\xi_{z}}=\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\xi)\,{\bf r}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\xi,\eta)\;\text{.}

If η∈Ωk,m\eta\in\Omega_{k,m} and ξ∈Δk,m+1\xi\in\Delta_{k,m+1} (such that ηx≥2\eta_{x}\geq 2), we have

(B.4) ςα^,k​(η)​𝐫α^,k𝒜​(η,ξ)=cx​y​ηx​α^y​∏z∈Vηz>0α^zηz=cx​y​ξx​ξy​∏z∈Vξz>0α^zξz=ςα^,k​(ξ)​𝐫kℬ​(ξ,η)​.\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\eta)\,{\bf r}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\eta,\xi)=c_{xy}\,\eta_{x}\hat{\alpha}_{y}\,\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in V\\ \eta_{z}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{\hat{\alpha}_{z}}{\eta_{z}}=c_{xy}\,\xi_{x}\xi_{y}\,\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in V\\ \xi_{z}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{\hat{\alpha}_{z}}{\xi_{z}}=\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\xi)\,{\bf r}^{\mathcal{B}}_{k}(\xi,\eta)\;\text{.}

If η,ξ∈Δk,m+1\eta,\xi\in\Delta_{k,m+1}, we have

(B.5) ςα^,k​(η)​𝐫kℬ​(η,ξ)=cx​y​ηx​ηy​∏z∈Vηz>0α^zηz=cx​y​ξx​ξy​∏z∈Vξz>0α^zξz=ςα^,k​(ξ)​𝐫kℬ​(ξ,η)​.\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\eta)\,{\bf r}^{\mathcal{B}}_{k}(\eta,\xi)=c_{xy}\,\eta_{x}\eta_{y}\,\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in V\\ \eta_{z}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{\hat{\alpha}_{z}}{\eta_{z}}=c_{xy}\,\xi_{x}\xi_{y}\,\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in V\\ \xi_{z}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{\hat{\alpha}_{z}}{\xi_{z}}=\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\xi)\,{\bf r}^{\mathcal{B}}_{k}(\xi,\eta)\;\text{.}

This shows that ςα^,k\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k} is reversible for the Markov chain described in (B.1), restricted to Ωk,m∪Δk,m+1\Omega_{k,m}\cup\Delta_{k,m+1}. Furthermore, by (5.15), we have, for all distinct η,ξ∈Ωk,m\eta,\xi\in\Omega_{k,m},

(B.6) ςα^,k(η)𝐫α^,kℳ(η,ξ)=ςα^,k(η)∑ζ∈Δk,m+1𝐫α^,k𝒜(η,ζ)𝐏ζℬ[τξ=τΩk].\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\eta)\,{\bf r}^{\mathcal{M}}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\eta,\xi)=\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\eta)\sum_{\zeta\in\Delta_{k,m+1}}{\bf r}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\eta,\zeta)\,{\bf P}_{\zeta}^{\mathcal{B}}\,[\tau_{\xi}=\tau_{\Omega_{k}}]\;\text{.}

Following (ℬk​(t))t≥0(\mathcal{B}_{k}(t))_{t\geq 0}, from ζ∈Δk,m+1\zeta\in\Delta_{k,m+1} to arrive at ξ∈Ωk,m\xi\in\Omega_{k,m}, the trajectory must stay in Δk,m+1\Delta_{k,m+1}. Thus, by reversibility, the right-hand side is equal to

(B.7) ςα^,k(ξ)∑ζ∈Δk,m+1𝐫α^,k𝒜(ξ,ζ)𝐏ζℬ[τη=τΩk]=ςα^,k(ξ)𝐫α^,kℳ(ξ,η).\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\xi)\sum_{\zeta\in\Delta_{k,m+1}}{\bf r}^{\mathcal{A}}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\xi,\zeta)\,{\bf P}_{\zeta}^{\mathcal{B}}\,[\tau_{\eta}=\tau_{\Omega_{k}}]=\varsigma_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\xi)\,{\bf r}^{\mathcal{M}}_{\hat{\alpha},k}(\xi,\eta)\;\text{.}

This concludes the proof of the lemma. ∎
